THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Oral History -- Arnett Cobb
Sides 1-4

Interview by Stanley Dance &
Helen Oakley Dance

Washington, D. C.
August, 1978
March 18, 1978

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
-- how many times we've had you (unintelligible)
Oh, a million times.
I didn't know.
And worse than that, you get home sometimes and you've got a BLANK TICKET. (unintelligible)
Oh, yes, oh, yes.

If you could, (unintelligible) I'll hold it, ARNETT, THEN YOU WOULD BE FREE - THEN I CAN MOUNT IT LIKE THAT I think if we can start at the beginning, this is Arnett Cobb on March the -- what's the date?
This is March 18th.
That's right; 1978.
That's the year.
And we're going to ask you to begin with where you were born and when.
I was born in Houston, Texas in the year of 1918, August 10. And that gives a little indication of my age, when you said 1978. It makes me 59 now, until August 10th.
Yeah, that's right. So then you have to take a couple off for a year or two.
Well, I'll get up to 60 and be very proud and I'm going to tell you why later, and the older I get the prouder I get. I'll tell you why I'm glad.
Now, were your parents musical?
My grandmother taught piano.
Oh. So your mother played, too.
She played, too. My uncle played. Had a couple or three of the ten kids that played, the ones that were interested; I'll put it like that.

You only get out of life what you put into it and if you apply yourself, you're going to get it, but if you're not going to apply yourself, you're not going to get it. So the ones that applied themselves got it.
So my mother was one; my uncle was one; and another aunt was one; and that was it. I don't how I came through.
You died when your -- your father died when you were six.
Six years old.
And you barely remember him.

I vaguely remember him, but I had something to remember him by. He gave me a Chesterfield overcoat, and I don't know Stanley, if you know what a Chesterfield overcoat, to my knowledge, what it was, but it had the fur around the collar.
Yeah.

You know, and it was kind of -- something down the -- but it was gray with the black fur around it and I was the sharpest little youngster and I was proud of me and I'd go out there and say, 'See my new coat?' You know, I'm proud. I'd get a pair of new shoes and I'd say -- my mother'd say, 'Come

" " here, boy, sit down. " See my new shoes? " I let everybody know anything I had new, in church, anywhere. I was proud of it. That was my nature. I didn't know it then. I found out later. And anything I got new I'd like to share it with everybody today.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Well, Arnett, when your father died, was that when you went to live with your friend's grandfather.
No. I was already there.
Oh, you were already there.
Yes, because he and my mother wasn't together.
Oh, I've got you, yeah.

And my mother was a domestic worker but he did this for me because, like all fathers would do, or some, showing their interest, you know. But I don't think it was two or three months later that he passed, but he was sick during that time, my mother told me. In later years she told me how it happened. And he died of tuberculosis.
Your grandfather, he had a really large family.

He had ten kids, seven girls, three boys. And he was a man that believed in living under his roof, you live by my law. And that's the way it went down. And he would buy food -- he'd feed you, you couldn't pay him anything. I
don't care if you had a job. You don't pay him anything to stay there, and he'll feed you because he bought everything in gross lots for his family.
What did he do for a living?
He was a boiler maker.
Oh.

For (unintelligible) Boiler Works here in Houston, Texas. And I guess that he had a good salary if he could buy crates of eggs, ten pounds packs of potatoes, and what have you. That's the way he bought it. He didn't buy no little small lots for ten children, you know.

But I want to say this to you, Stanley: During that time, you could go out if you want pan sausage, you could get it for four cents a pound. Get a loaf of bread for three cents. And we could get five pounds of pan sausage on the corner at the corner grocery store for 20 cents and feed a lot of people, in those days. But even then my grandfather didn't do it. He went another route and got it cheaper than that. Can you imagine? Four cents a pound, three cents for a loaf of bread.
I am telling you the factual truth about --
Well, look at the way prices have doubled in the last ten years of a lot of things.
Well, we'd go so far as to talk about prices, the American dollar, I just heard the other day that the American dollar now is worth 26 cents.
(Inaudible) [THAT'S UNBELIEVABLE]
Isn't that beautiful?
(Inaudible) well, that's exactly...
Twenty-six cents! So what are you getting for your money? Nothing.
(Unintelligible) IT'S THE SAME WAY WITH THE POUND
And wait another few more years, then it won't be worth nothing and what the heck you doing? You're out there knocking your brains out for nothing.

Well, of course, you know what it does do. It makes the idea of saving your money seem a bit stupid in a way because if you save a dollar today with the idea that you'll have that in ten years' time, in ten years' time it's --
It'll multiply.
Yeah, it's multiplied, but it's also lost so much value, you've got where you started.
Right.
You were saying earlier, though, that your father ran a very strict house with the TIME
My grandfather.
Your grandfather with the time when the kids had to be in at night.
So I had a young uncle -- see, his curfew -- he had curfew hours for ones of certain ages for
12:00 o'clock that was of that age, and the ones that were older, 1:00 o'clock. So that made an hour differential in the two different age groups.

So one night my young uncle had the 1:00 o'clock curfew and once that it happened, he'd slip that key and that's it, you're locked out. And the girls let him through a window. He knew what the policy was so he didn't -- it's not like he'd come and knock on the door and get in. He didn't want Papa to know nothing about nothing. He (unintelligible) and them girls let him in, but he knew he was in there.
WENT TO THE WINDOW AND KNOCKED ON THE WINDOW

The next day he come home from his work. He had platted some leather and made a good whip out of it. And knotted it on the end in three plats. And when he walked in the door he just started to lash it. Pow Pow Pow. He said, "Papa, what you doing?" He said, "I told you if you live under my roof, you'll abide by my law." He said, "Well, Papa, I'm grown up." "If you're that grown, get your THINGS packed up and get out." So he did. He packed up and got out and never come back anymore. That was a stern, firm father. You know, what they say today, that's the wrong way to go.
Well, did he never come back at all?
Not even to --
No, sir.
-- talk --
I said, no, sir. He made his own life until
death. He died in '45 and I was in Washington, D. C. at the Howard Theater when my mother called me and told me he passed.
Well, I mean, did any of you kids who knew him (unintelligible) ever see him?
We saw him, sure.
Oh, you did. Yeah, I see. You just didn't --
But his father didn't see him.
Oh, I've got you.

And his father didn't look for him after he told him to get out. He didn't for his father after he told him to get out. That's how firm the situation was. But he was -- my grandfather was a man that stood on his own convictions, meant every word he said. And that's the way it was.
Well, now, when do you start sort of -- you did say the school was very near where you lived with your grandfather, didn't you?
Well, the elementary school --
Yeah.
-- was a block and a half away.
Well, that was pretty nice.
Darn close.
Yes.
Walking distance.
That's right. When did you start to
sort of get into music?

Well, let me tell you. I'll give you the rundown on that. I come out of elementary at the end of it and went into the 7th grade at Phyllis Wheatley High School in Houston. And, of course, as time grew for a couple of years there, they formed a band. I was interested in the band, but by the same token they had a project like a lot of people do come to the schools to sell you an idea to take 50 lessons at a dollar a lesson once a week for 50 weeks, you get the violin free.
So I was in on that project and I took 50 lessons.
On the violin?
On the violin. Right here in Houston at the Ben Zindler (Phonetic) Building, every Saturday for 50 weeks.
How far from where you lived was that?
Pardon?
How far from where you lived was that?
I had to take the street car, what we call -- which is the trolley car.
Yeah.
We call it street car.
We call it a tram.
Well, good, we have different words for it.
Same thing.
But it -- you could ride it and get off right in front of the building from where I stayed coming down Nance street.
What was the name of the building?
Ben Zindler.
How do you spell that?
You can spell Ben, but the Zindler is Z-i-n-d-l-e-r.
I see.
One of the sons on television on Channel 13 in Houston.
Oh.
And he's a trouble shooter. Anybody that's wrong in Houston, write him and he'll screen them out.
You were saying you were living on Nash Street?
Nance, N-a-n-c-e.
Oh, right, Ray Nance.
Right, like Ray Nance.
Yeah.
How did you associate that?
Well, tell me how -- I mean, what was -- we're talking --
Let's don't get too far from what we're
talking about on the violin.
I just --
I took the 50 lessons.
But I just want to ask you something about Houston at that time. We're talking of what? 1930?
In the '30s.
Yeah. Well, I mean, Houston was a much smaller city then because, you know --
Houston was a country town.
It was, yeah.
But I didn't know it until later because I wasn't smart enough to know it. I was too young.
All right, but you had street cars. So now you take 50 lessons on the violin.
Yes, sir. And get back to Houston, my mother used to say the country (unintelligible), she said this is going to be one of the greatest metropolitan cities of the South. My mother said that.
Why did she say that?
Why did she think that?

I don't know. My mother lived in New York and ride the subway and people thought she had a sixth sense and she wouldn't bother nobody and they'd come over and ask her to tell them about themselves. She said, 'I don't know nothing about you.' But what she visualized was her

SITUATION.
(unintelligible).
I mean the big development of Houston has been since World War II, hasn't it really?

I wasn't here. I tell you what my mother says, Stan, and I want you to hear this, and I want you to look at Houston today, you can, and I think about what she said. She didn't pass until '75. She got to see some of it. But her predictions were very good, and she's no Nancy Dixon, I don't think. (Jeanne Dixon--ed.)
Well, when you lived on Nance Street, was that sort of in the city or was that getting out a bit?
What is that, now?
When you lived on Nance Street -
No. I was in the city.
Oh, it was in the city?
I was only ten minutes from town.
Well, now, let's get back to the violin.
All right.
How did you like it?
I liked everything I did during those days because it was activities for me and it was very interesting. I took the 50 lessons; my mother financed it. And I got it and I got my violin free.
But I went into Phyllis Wheatley High School Band
with an 80-piece brass band and I'm the only fiddle player in there.
And no amplifier.
And I couldn't hear myself play.
No.
You listen to what I say.
Yeah, I know what you're saying.

But I'm happy to be there. I'm SAWING and SAWING and so finally the instructor says, he says, "Son, wouldn't you like to have a horn?" I said, "I sure would." He said, "Okay, we got one left." It was a C melody saxophone. Now, what did I know between a C melody anything, Stanley. But I had to get it and I was ready to take it then. He said, "No, I got to get a confirmation from your parents that somebody will be responsible for it." I'm just a kid.
How old were you, Arnett?

This time I must have been about 12 or 13 years old, because I started playing professionally at 14. That's how fast it was. He said, "No, you can't take it out today. Bring me a note from your mother or your parents, anybody, tomorrow." And I brought it from my mother. I said, "I know she'll stand for it." And she did. And they let me take it out. C melody. I was so happy with it. I played My Country Tis of Thee." I knew the notes from piano, violin, so all I had to do was learn the fingering of the horn.
I played this thing for a while and just as happy. I marched up Armistice Day down Main Street playing my horn with the lyre and the music, all that, and what have you and enjoyed myself. Happy.

Finally, one day in Phyllis Wheatley High School where I attended and graduated in 1935, my first class to me was rotten and I had a teacher that was so firm -- she was a Christian Scientist. She didn't believe in you getting sick or nothing. And the tenor saxophone player took sick and we were playing -- the band was playing at the Ethiopian Cafe on Mylom (phonetic) and I wanted to be in that band so bad I didn't know what to do. He took sick, God bless him.
The what band was playing?
Phyllis Wheatly High School stage band.
That were playing at the --
But I wasn't playing in it. I had C melody and it didn't fit.
I see. How big was this stage band?
Oh, it was 16 or 17 pieces.
Oh, I see.
But we're playing stock arrangements.
Yeah, well, I mean it was a band out of the sort of marching band.
No, no, no, I'm not talking about the marching band. I'm talking about the stage band that's playing
music for dinner music and this sort of thing.
Or dancing.
Dance band.
I got you, yeah.
Which we call stage band.
Right.

All right. I'm in the first class which Agry COLA, which is a fan MR. PUELLA, PUELLA, I don't like (unintelligible) girl and boy, Latin. What the hell I need with Latin? What -- I'm not going to be a doctor. And she's -- that's my first period class. And I'm not lying to you. And they sent a message in there, please release Arnett Cobb to come down and rehearse with the stage band. And she said, Arnett Cobb, you are excused to go down to the auditorium for rehearsal with the band. I said, 'Thank you,' and they put me on tenor saxophone. No more C melody. That's how I got the tenor. And the young man that took sick could never play no more. The doctor told him he couldn't play anymore and I fell heir to the horn. That's how I happen to play tenor today.
Well, now, Arnett, going from C melody to tenor, that wasn't as simple as that, was it?
Yeah.
It was?
Very simple to me. Because the mechanism of the situation was the same. The only difference was the
key signature.
Yeah.
C melody is a C horn just like piano. But the tenor is a B flat instrument --
Yeah.
-- which is, as you know, a tone above the piano.
Right.
ALL RIGHT, But that doesn't make any difference what your key instrument is, as long as it's an instrument that you can play in jazz.
Well --
But C melody, they don't use it in jazz bands.
NO: (Unintelligible)
But, see, I didn't know that then either. I found all this out later. Isn't that something how you can learn later on? Helen, don't look at me in that tone of voice.
C melody, though, it kind of can sound pretty, can't it?
I think it can sound pretty, but, see, I never really concentrated on it after I left it. Now, I'm talking about the '30s now, Stanley, and that's a long time ago. Now, if you bring me one today --
Yeah.
-- I'll let you know more about it because I have more knowledge about what's going on.
Well, I was wondering, you know, what -- you know, I really don't know much about the C melody.
Well, does it sound anything like the soprano saxophone?
It's between the soprano and the alto, isn't it?
Yeah.
But what I really meant was, doesn't it have a kind --
May I tell you something?
Yeah.
It's strictly for marching band, that's all it's for.
Oh, I see.
That's all it is.
No, but I wondered whether it had a character of its own which was -- there's somebody who's playing that now -- oh, you know that boy, the clarinet player, Kenny DAVERN?
Yeah.
I think he's playing a C melody now.
Yeah, I READ THAT somewhere (unintelligible)
Who is that?

There was a boy called Kenny DAUSBN, plays clarinet; they had what they called Soprano -- he and BAB Wilbur were both playing soprano (Soprano Summit+--ed.) saxophones. And somebody told me that he was playing C melody. I just wondered what sort of sound he'd get on it.
C melody could be maybe a beautiful instrument, but it's not a known instrument to jazz musicians today. And nobody's ever thought of it. It could be an instrument maybe today that might be superb.
Well, I mean, the sop--
Now, let me give you the association with C melody. C melody and oboe go with the same thing.
Oh.
And that's how I had at that time in school among my associates and friends -- they called me Obay instead of oboe because C melody and oboe was the same.
This is the --
In sound and key.
Hey, we've missed something, This is the second nickname you've got, because you said your grandfather called you Rooster.
Rooster. I've got more before it's over with.
We'll come to that.
Yeah. But I'm just letting you know
coming up the stair steps.
Well, I want you to remember.
And they called me Obay in high school.
Did -- do you remember, didn't Frankie Trumbauer play C melody? I think he did.
No, I don't remember -- I remember him as an alto player.
Yeah.
And, of course, Frankie wrote a lot of musical books.
I thought -- I (unintelligible) HAVE A FEELING
I wouldn't deny you in what you say, but I don't know. I know of his alto works.
Yeah. Well, that's what he's famous for.
Yeah. Right.
So, anyway, you get on the tenor and you like it, I guess.
Stanley, I haven't been off it since and don't intend to get off of it. That has been my bread and butter over a period of years and I've been in this business now about 47 years this year.
Did you ever have any doubles, I mean, or did you just --
Yes, I doubled. I doubled bass clarinet

in Lionel Hampton's band. I have it here now. I run into a guy going into the Army (IN THE 40's) (unintelligible) and he wanted to get rid of the horn and I didn't know what a bass clarinet was. I'd never seen one before in my life. To be so stupid. And he told me he'd sell it to me for $75.00. I said, "$75.00 for this?" He said, "Yeah." I didn't know the value of a -- I'm ignorant about this. Yeah, he's going in the Army and he could -- he isn't going to come out anymore. He's going across-- you know, he (unintelligible) I guess he did. So I bought it.

I had to go to Gladys Hampton and get the money. I didn't have it. That's Lionel Hampton's wife. But I bought it. I've got it right here now in my closet. I have used it on occasion, but I doubled on it in Hamp's band where Milt Rube Buckner wrote things behind vocalists like Rube Blakeley, maybe Dinah Washington on ballads, maybe Madeline Green, maybe Winnie Brown. I'm talking about mostly on vocal tunes or ballads, and you had all clarinets and a bass clarinet, just like you got all the saxophones and a baritone sax to anchor. I was the anchor man. Okay.
Did you like playing it?
Love it.
It's a pretty instrument.
Love it.
Yeah.
So I learned the principles. You have
different principles in that. And, of course, as you get older -- and I had guys that taught me out of -- of course your registers are different.
Yeah.
And the bottom is one register and when you get up the top, it's just like the saxophone, but it's not like the saxophone on the bottom.
THAT'S WHY A CLARINET'S A HARD INSTRUMENT TO PLAY.
So how did you do it. It's a hard instrument, isn't it?
If you learned clarinet first, you'd be better off to pick up a saxophone after alto, but I didn't learn it first.

Now, I'm gonna give you something else. Here in Houston, when I come up in the thirties, we didn't have no instructors. I'm a self made musician. We had one guy that knew theory and could teach it --but he was so busy, he didn't have the time. The whites wouldn't accept you as a black. Are you listening good?
Yeah. I know what you're saying.

All right. Abner Jones was his name, and we had a theatre here, this was during the silent movie days; it was a trio that played for the silent movies, and he was the drummer, and the xylophone player -- I didn't say vibraphone -- I said xylophone.
Yeah, I know.
So it was piano, drums, and the other guy was a violin player. Anderson Lacy, And we'd look at the silent movies, and they'd play the prettiest music -- but they were good musicians.

Now that was the only man who could teach us any instrument, but he didn't have the time. Now, let me tell you what we learned from him. After I got with the Milton Larkin Loggins band, in 1936 is when I joined him. Milton Larkin.
Yeah, that makes you 18.
Pardon?
That makes you 18 years old?
No, I'm not 18 yet, now.
Now wait a minute. '36 . . . You were born in '18, he was
Now you've got to get your calculus together.
Yeah, I know.
No, you've right. If you were born in 1918...
Okay. I was born in 1918. I joined Milton in '36.
1936 is 18 years later.
Wait just a second. What did you do in between the time you were with this stage band and Larkin? Milt Loggins? Or did you go from the stage band to Milt?
No, no.
Oh, I thought ...
Let me tell you what happened. My first summer month that I went out professionally, I went out with

a guy from Louisiana by the name of Frank Davis, and this was in 1934 during the summer month when school was out. And, of course, I was the youngest guy in the group, at my age, and I have to think what age I was then, because you're turning me down; you can figure it by years if I was born in '18, and school month come out before August come in, and my birthday is August 10th, and of course, anywhere I went they'd have to come and consult my mother and be responsible for me as the leader.
That's the way it was. And if you didn't do that, I couldn't go, see? During those days, parents were strict, and mine were very strict.

Now, we went out like 3 months all over the state of Louisiana, because he is from Louisiana. I come back here and I go back to school in September. Now, on that band was a guy by the name of Chester Boone that liked my playing, and he had formed a band in Houston, and went into the Harlem Grill here in Houston, Texas.
You said Chuck Boone?
No, I said Chester. C-h-e-s-t-e-r, Chester Boone
Oh, Chester Boone. He was a saxophone player, wasn't he?
He was a trumpet player.
Well, there was a Chester Boone...
Chester Boone
But wasn't there a Chester Boone that was a saxophone player? (Lester Boone - ed.)
I don't know.
From Chicago?
I don't know, but I come back the same year, in '34, and he formed a band to go in to the Harlem Grill here in Houston on West Dallas for 6 nights a week. (unintelligible)
Wow.

Now my mother is working, making $10 a week, and I'm getting $34 a week for 6 nights a week. But the ironic situation was I went to worked at rehearsal for the job and went home to do my studies for school, and take me a nap and go to work and missed the first night! I knew I lost my job, but I didn't.

I woke up in 2 o'clock in the morning, and Helen, you didn't hear me, did you? everything was finis then. Well, I'm telling the truth. But I was all right after that. And I stayed with Chester for 2 years -- from '34 to '36, and that's when I transferred and went over ... (end TAPE SIDE 1)

... pieces. And we went up to Dallas, and I took sick up there. And I was a guy that believed in taking my money and putting it in a sock, and putting a safety pin in it, and when I put the safety pin in it, that means one thing. Don't spend it. But I neglected myself, and took sick. I didn't eat properly.
I see. Yeah. You were trying to save too much.
Yeah.
What were you, about 17 then?
I don't know ... it was in '34.
I mean, Wah -- before you ...
I'm gonna let you all figure it, because I ain't that good in mathematics. I took 18½ months of accounting, but when you pinpoint me, I have to get a pencil and paper.
Well, it was '34.

'34. And, he had to get permission -- I was young enough for him to get permission from my mother to take me away, and somebody said they saw me on crutches up there, and that was twice -- and Chester loved those crutches, and everybody thought we were brothers. But not knowing that I was sick, too; I was in the bed and Chester got me out of the bed to come to the phone to talk to my mother, because her boyfriend said, 'I'll pay for this call'. And he put the coins in, and she asked me, 'Baby, how you doing?' And I'd say 'Fine.' Sick as a dog! And Stanley, I wouldn't lie to you. But he told me to say it, and I was a youngster, so what did I know?

He brought me in to Houston; I was weighing 172 pounds, and when I came back to Houston, I weighed 119½, and you could count every rib on my body. And when he come in that driveway and brought my mother from where she was working,
that was where he brought me. You know, I had pleurisy, and didn't even know it.
Oh?

Yes sir. I was getting ready to tell you something now. My mother felt like she wanted to kill him. She wanted to go and get her boss's gun and kill him. But I guess the presence of it pressed on her mind and she didn't do it. And when she carried me to the doctor, and they had what you call -- she was a tuberculosis specialist, but I had pleurisy. Dr. Robie. I don't know if she's dead or alive today. But that woman was something else.

But she told my mother and she examined me, and told her it was just a matter of time -- too late. That's medical science for you. I was 15. I can tell you how old I was then. I was 15 years old -- or 16. Somewhere in there, 15 or 16. And here I am, that young, gonna die with pleurisy?

And she put me in Jefferson Davis Hospital here, but first she come to my house, hit me with them big needles, about half as big as my little finger, and shoot that dope in me, or whatever it was, and I could feel them pushing on me, you know. But they were pumping fluid up there, and she came to my house first. You don't have anybody come to your house today -- you know that, don't you?
But she came to my house and did it. Had a pan and shoot that fluid out to me, and then after she got it to a certain level, she brought me to the hospital. And I ain't
dead yet! I'm 59 years old today. Medical science said I was dead.
Today you're 59?
I'm 59 until August the 10th and I'll be 60. Now Stanley, are you getting your mathematics together? I was born in 1918; August 10th.
No, but when you said you were 59 today I thought you were ...
No, I say I'm 59 now.
What I was thinking now was, of course, with your family, your mother must have been very worried about you because of your problem. Age.

You know what she said to me after I came out of this thing? She said, 'Baby, the only thing I could do was pray, and I was so worried when they had given you up for dead and said it was just a matter of time.' And she said, 'I was over the sink one day, and I was washing the dishes where I'm working, and the only thing I could say, was I just prayed, and said, 'God, whatever your will is, let it be' --' and she said everything lifted off her shoulders after she said that.
Your mother was ... what religion was she?
She was Baptist, just like me.
So you were brought up as a Baptist?
All the way. Still is.
Were you sort of then very strictly brought up with that religion?
Strictly?
Yeah.
It was a must.
It was?

But Milt did most of the writing. Of course, Milt got no credit for anything he did.

And I think I feel free today to say things that happened that I didn't think was right and -- in the music business. I'm in it, and I wouldn't want it done to me. But Curly Hamner came in the band, and Curly got a check for
$2,200.00 and Gladys got one for $2,200.00. Hamp got one for $2,200.00, and Milton Buckner did the tune, and he got 600.00.
Well, why did Curly get (inaudible)?
You're asking me questions, Stanley, I can't answer. I want to know why too. And he come in (inaudible) big long check from the record company. Or publishing company, I should have said.
Well, now, Curly, did he play drums (inaudible)?
Yes.
But he wasn't really a drummer, was he? I mean wasn't he --
Dancer.
Yes.

But he come in and got very influential. He's one of the reasons I left the band because people got gigs (inaudible) over that and disrespect-wise and everything. And I wasn't going to have mine around it. So I knew when to put my notice in, and I'll let you know about that too.
Well, Curly presumably has gotten his name on some of these numbers.
Huh?
Curly had gotten his name --
Came right (inaudible) he wouldn't know a note if he saw one, but he got paid for something he didn't --

and, see, this is -- I don't think it's right. And I'm not there now, and I could afford to say it, and you can blast it if you want to. That's taking money for -- Arnett Cobb's (inaudible) money for and Swing and never received a quarter. That's Hamp and company.
Don't you have your name on it?
I got copyright on it.
Well, how come they didn't give you the money?
You asking me? Go ask him. Ga-ga-ga-g-g-- he's always got some excuse. That's how come he's a millionaire and I'm not.
Yeah, but --
I get bitter about these things today.
(Inaudible).
Because you're taking something from somebody that doesn't belong to you.
Yeah, but you really (inaudible) talking about it (inaudible) that's very funny because that must be the record company.

I can go -- I'm going to give you some more about this. I signed a contract with Hamp for two years, had my first contract at so much money. And on my second contract I signed for two years he had me in a lawyer's office in California. Garden was his name, Lawyer Garden.

And he brought both me and my wife over . He had a box of stockings for my wife. He had a fifth of something for me. I don't know what it was. And in this contract that he was to pay me so much a week, travel me first class and to bill me, to bill the band at the expiration of this contract and put -- finance me with $5,000.00, and he's going to have 50 percent of it.
All right, Gladys was grooving me what the band business was. Now, I was pretty close to (inaudible). But my first class transportation wasn't it. I didn't get it. I still rode in the coach.
Well, that saved some money.

Just on the contract. There's always an excuse why. And I ended up -- the best thing I got first class transportation was we were leaving California, and they come in another route, and they gave me and my wife the drawing room (inaudible) and gave me all the tickets for the band to be in charge, and we had a car all the time, said that's the first first class transportation we ever had.

And everybody was assigned to the berths, seniority low berth, upper berth for the later ones that come in, and my wife and I had the drawing room where normally Gladys or Hamp would have had if they were there. And this was a big deal, I mean going from there into Kansas City, because we were playing at the auditorium now. And it was an enjoyable
trip. And this is when both of them came down to the train to see us off. This was unusual. (Inaudible) see nobody off.
(Inaudible) keep referring to Gladys, and that's Lionel Hampton's wife.
Say what now?
Well, I'm just saying on here that the reference is to Gladys, to Lionel Hampton's wife.
Right.
So that's clear.

And she was the one that was instructing me, because, see, Gladys had got her schooling from Benny Goodman, because Benny Goodman hired her to come and take care of him. That was the last alternative. And I heard this out of her mouth. She told that in Columbus, Ohio. And she was working for Joan Crawford, movie star, at the Modise.
Oh, that's what she was doing.

And she was getting $150.00 a week. Benny asked her, said, what are you getting. Now, what I'm saying to you I am quoting her. What do you get a week? She said, $150.00. He said, I'll pay you $150.00 to come and look (inaudible). Hamp had his wino friends coming around. He'd be late coming in, and they'd get ready to go (in-audible). He sent a plane ticket -- be here. Because Hamp had an audience (inaudible) wanted him, but he can't stand the situation of lateness.

And she said okay. She accepted it, and he paid her $150.00 a week to come and take care of him. And she'd go out there (inaudible) some of his friends, say, I'm sorry, man; he going to eat. Come back -- sorry, man, he's going back to do his show. Get off at night, sorry, man, he's going home to rest, and she excluded him by his friends, and that was what her job was to be.
That's how that began, huh?

Yeah, I'm telling you like (inaudible) how it was. That's the way it was. Finally Hamp ran into the Christian Sciencstage, and he cut all his (inaudible) to drinking and all that, and he keep his Christian Science books with him, and he's a successful man today because of it. But before that he was a wino, Gladys said. He slept on pool tables in California and everything. Gladys was the only one could handle him.
When did they get married?
I don't know.
(Inaudible).
Married before '36. I'll tell you that. He worked for Benny Goodman for four years, in '36 until '40. He was on that Camel Caravan, as you remember.
Well, he was telling me that they got married. They were going to drive from L.A. to New York to join Benny Goodman, and they got married on the way
Yeah. Okay.
I mean apart from (inaudible) he was an exciting musician.
And still is.
Yeah. Yeah.
You can't take nothing from him on that.
(Inaudible).

Right. Right. And love what he done. Only one bad feature about him that I disliked, he wants his musicians (inaudible) what you call rehearsals. He might rehearse another (inaudible) and end up playing the first one. But he keep you there all day.

And I said this. The man was lonely. He didn't have the right thing with him -- you know, his marriage -- so he needed a band with him, somebody where he could play his instrument (inaudible) that he had the control over and (inaudible) so he called rehearsal.
We left Kansas City on a cattle car and (inaudible) going to Oakland. Hamp and Gladys catches the Chief and go out.
(Inaudible) cattle car?
Cattle car, when I say (inaudible) seats, sitting up. No -- sleep the best way you can.
Yeah.

We get in to Oakland and pull in, and Hamp's at the station. (Inaudible) rehearsal at 6:00 o'clock. Yes, he did. Yes, he did. Don't care nothing about you. He's rested. He went in on the fast route. Now he want his band to be at the auditorium in Oakland to rehearse at 6:00, and we ain't even got our rooms yet. And we're getting in at 4:00 o'clock in the evening.
Not a bite to eat, eating sandwiches on the train.
Well, don't the guys tell him something?

Joe Wilder did. He said, dog dablits -- (inaudible) that's the way he cussed -- dog gablits, I won't be there. I'll be there for whatever time you're going to start up (inaudible) be there,and he was the first one there warming up.
Dog Gablits?
Dog Gablits, that's a cussing word for him.
(Laughter)

Dad Gommit, oh, he was a big cusser. But he uses a word one day and not (inaudible) that was that Hamp called rehearsal, and Joe was stirred up, and him and Hamp got (inaudible), and finally Hamp told him k-k-k-k-k-k-kiss my ass. And Joe said, you kiss my a-arse too.
(Laughter)
And the band fell out. He couldn't even say it properly, aa-aa-arse.
Well, that's English for ass, you know.
(Laughter)
But -- Well, what kind of a guy is Joe Wilder then?
One of the sweetest and finest guys you ever want to meet in your life --
Well, I know it, but --
-- and can play too.
Yeah, but you'd never think he would be the one to -- I mean he's usually very quiet, isn't he?

Always he's quiet. But Joe is a guy that (inaudible) he going to beat you to the job and warm up for one hour before he hit. That's why he never split a note. He's ready when the band get there. But, see, Joe Wilder was the first solo cornetist in the Philadelphia Symphony.
Oh, is that what he was.

Very trained. And he come up to Dizzy one night in Philadelphia and asked him could he sit in, had his horn under his arm, and Diz said, sure, come on up, boy. He didn't know Joe from anybody else, and Joe got up there and played. He said, where (inaudible) upset Dizzy's nerve. Joe
is too much.
That's nice.

Hear what I'm saying to you. I'm tell -- see, Joe Wilder and I joined the band at the same time in San Francisco, Hamp's band. And they isolated us, and we were roommates on the road, two newest guys in the band. Joe took Carl George's place. And I took Illinois' place, and the syndicate was for Illinois and Carl George because that was the Joe Newman was with this.

And give you a strange thing about Joe Newman, they all looking at Joe and, you know, they don't know. We were on our way back, going towards East, going towards Chicago, and we got into Denver. We played Denver a night. Joe had been there a long time and going to have some fun. So he told -- he said to Hamp, said, why don't you call 102, signifying. 102 was Trumpet Reveille that Milton Buckner did with 64ths in it and everything.

So Joe looked at Curly. Hamp said, ch-ch-ch-ch-- (inaudible) we're going to have to rehearse. And Joe looked and said, you could knock it off. That's how trained he was. Playing -- he played it verbatim. He looked at it, and from that point on they all respected Joe. You couldn't get Joe Newman off of Wilder. He was asking questions, and before everything was significant, like, you know, (inaudible). But he showed them something.
How long does this go on for a newcomer in the band?
I don't know, but they would leave us, and they would say (inaudible). They knew where they were going. We were new in the band. We had to feel our way. But we stuck together.
Well, did that happen in any other band?

I don't know. I never had that experience with anybody because this is the first big band because I told you our band, Milton (inaudible) band was a family band. And this is one thing I feel, but with Joe being with me, with Joe Wilder being with me, we -- we've -- we handled it pretty well, and they get their cabs and leave us, don't tell us where they're going, where to stop or nothing. And that's how isolated they were, and they syndicated different things.
It's a good thing you weren't alone.
Well, I had Joe with me, and we finally found our way. And I tell you one thing. Today I know my way around anywhere I go.
(Laughter)
And I made friends. Yeah, well, I mean you were both able to take care of yourself musically, so there was that,
(inaudible).

I've got some news for you. I just left New York. And I'm with a group of guys. We've got it going now all right. But it's the same difference. They go their own respective ways. They don't care nothing about you. But, see, if I didn't know my way around New York or Jersey, they would be treating me wrong, but I'm all right now. And today they're all selfish, and I can't understand selfish musicians.
People don't have (inaudible).
When you come to Houston, I'm not selfish with you. I invite you to my house.
(Inaudible).
But you catch them and -- oh, when you come to New York, call them -- call them, they're busy doing nothing.
Well --
See what I say, I mean nothing.
That's so very --

But I need them like I need another hole in the head, Ellen, because I have to make my own way. They made me do this. I had guys that come down to Houston that I admired, respected, and I'm in the buzzard group. You know what the buzzard group is? In the Majestic Theater where Blacks had to go to catch the Cab Callaways, the Lucky Millinders, the Jimmie Luncefords, you listen to me, unless I
went backstage, and the only band I went backstage on was Jimmy Lunceford's because of Joe Thomas.
What do you mean, the buzzards?
How do you --
In the roof up there.
Oh, the roof.
I call it the buzzard roof.
Roof --
Roost, yeah.
Roof, r-o-o-f, not roost.
Not roost, oh.

MR. COBB: Roof, because that's where it was. It was in the roof, right next to the ceiling upstairs, as high as the theater was. That's where we had to sit, and we went in a different entrance. And all the acts on the show, man, was first class. Oh, I just enjoyed this, and I wasn't (inaudible). I got to New York and saw these same people that I admired bagging for a couple of dollars. You hear me talking to you. You don't believe it.

I'm at the Apollo Theater. Here I am admiring them. Here they come and asking me for some money, and I'm working as a side man in Lionel Hampton, and they'd starve in Houston. But in New York there was nothing. I didn't know that. See how you can be deceived and be disillusioned? And this is when I made up my mind. I said, this what it takes to deceive

people and be disillusioned. I'm going to start saving. Why, I don't want to be in this position no time down the road, and I started to prepare for (inaudible). I told you yesterday I took sick, had the spinal operation, had to go back and have it over, and when I come out of the hospital and I'd never gone to Ben Barr's office for the petty cash or nothing, I had one $700.00 left out of my savings and took part of that and bought a uniform for my band to start over again.
I made (inaudible).
Well, on that (inaudible) was Lucky Thompson in those days? This is --
You're asking me a question.
Yeah.
Lucky been playing about three years when he come with Hamp's band and could play very good for three years. He come out of Wilberforce University in Ohio. But very cocky.
Oh, he was cocky.
Very cocky.
Oh.

And he had gotten to the point, and it was a hassle that he and Hamp was -- no reason at all, and I wasn't guilty of the fact that what had happened. He had wanted a new horn, and he had gone to Gladys and asked Gladys to pay for the horn. He'd pay her back, and she said, okay,

man, I'll do that.

We were at this time, in 1943, in the Famous Door in New York, and the night that we opened up there, they had Benny Goodman, had all the stars, Billy Eckstine, Lena Horne, Georgia Auld, Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong. I mean the works. That opening night was terrific. I blew my neck off my horn on Flying Home. I could (inaudible) I blew it off. So my horn was damaged. I had to rubber band it down and everything in the middle of the show. So I couldn't go downstairs and hit no low notes. So I had to stay uptown with it until I got through.

Now, Lucky is giving Gladys a fit, and his wife joins in after we get into a situation, and Gladys ain't getting no money at the end of the week. We had two weeks up there. We didn't make the second. We didn't make the second week because they had trouble.

Then Lucky's going to needle her for his horn.
Well, what kind of trouble happened?
Huh?
What kind of trouble was it? Why didn't you make the second week?
They wasn't paying off right.
You mean the club?
The club.
Oh, I see.
At the Famous Door?
That's what I said.
That's what I said.
Oh, this is (inaudible).
Gladys had a hassle with her money. You know, when she started to having a hassle with money, she cut you off. And needling, you can forget it. That was her principle, and she lived on it.
And Lucky chose a time like that --

But his wife joined in, and they all cussed Gladys out, both of them. So Gladys forgot him. Now, I'm having trouble with my horn. Lucky comes up to the Audubon Ballroom up on 166th Street and Audubon, near the Medical Center. And he done sold his horn and come to play Hamp's job with a clarinet. And Hamp said, ch-ch-ch-ch (inaudible). He said, well, I'm going to play clarinet until I get my tenor.

Gladys called me the next day. She said, Arnett, you need a horn, don't you? I said yes. She said, Go to Mannings and try that horn out and see if you like it. That's where Lucky was getting it. If you like it, call me up at home. Give my right hand to God.
I went to Mannings the next day, and I was suffering with mine, but I wasn't bugging nobody about it. I

went there and tried the horn, and I called her up from Mannings. And I say I like it. She said, go to Joe Glazer's office to pick up the check and come back and get your horn, and that's what I did. $265.00. Went to Joe Glazer's office on 5th Avenue, come back to Mannings, pick my horn up and got in (inaudible) studio (inaudible), and Lucky recognized the horn by serial number, and he said I run down (inaudible). And I didn't even know that was his horn that he had picked.
What did he tell you?
Oh, he got mad at me. He told me I was a Tom this and -- Uncle Tom. I don't even know this is his horn, Ellen. Gladys told me to go over and try one out.
But what --

But, see, what had happened, Lucky and his wife done give her a fit, so she said, the heck with him, and, you know, Gladys is cold. She was cold when she want to be cold. So she said, I'll show him something. That's what she said.
Arnett, what would that horn have been worth new?
Huh?
What would that horn -- you said it was 265.00.
It was a used horn. It's second hand.
What would it have been worth new
About 500.00.
Oh, so it was a very good buy.
Yeah, because my wife bought me one Christmas '47 for 500.00 in Detroit. I got it now, and that one I won't get rid of.
What kind of horn was it?
Selmer.
Oh. You always played Selmer?
I bought one in Paris, and this is the Yamaha, endorsed that, got that for nothing. But I got to keep it because I'm selling them for the Yamaha people.
What happened to -- what happened as far as the upbeat on the horn was concerned? What did he do?
Well, he finally got his notice.
And never got the horn?

I had it. So he come in with clarinet. But he goes to show them up. I'm going to sell my horn off, and I'll come with a clarinet until you get my horn from them, but they didn't get it for them. So Hamp said, s-s-s-s-s-- gave -- and they gave him his notice.
Well (inaudible).
No, I just put that (inaudible).
Oh, I'm sorry. No, but why I asked
you about that was, you know, I knew he was like this later, but I didn't know when he --
Was like that then.
Oh, it must have been --
Didn't have but three years of experience on the horn.
That's strange because, you know, in some ways Lucky's very nice.

See, he's one of the guys that I taught that Lady Be Good to, and he'd catch on very fast, got a good, sharp mind, you know. But he had an attitude because I was giving it to him, so I -- you know, I'd been a fixture in the band for a while, so it didn't bother me.
But it -- you know, it seems to me as though Lucky was his own worst enemy really.
That's right.
You know, I know, you know when --
That's why he had to leave and go to Europe.

Yeah, because he -- I mean a lot of the things he said and did were -- were right in a way. We know the business was rotten. We know agents take advantage and everything, but still and all you have to be careful you're not cutting off your nose to spite your face.
And that's what he did. And behind that

he lost his wife. She passed. And he'd begin to say, here, now, he's back in New York, and he's doing fine. I tell you who loved him really, Archie Moore really loved Lucky. He was willing to put some money behind him and everything to make him go.

And he come to see me when I was flat on my back from my final operation, when I was living in Long Island at the time. And he was (inaudible) -- and he's just like Lucky's (inaudible). You know how you can get?
Is that right?
Yeah.
And he put money back of him?
No, he didn't. But he was willing to.
Yeah, I understand.

But by this time Lucky was getting ready to leave out of the country because he had -- you know, you can overtalk yourself and treat people wrong, and no booking office in New York would touch him from his attitude. See, you got to play ball sometime. You got to be a nice guy sometime, especially if your foot ain't in the door. But once you get your foot in the door, you might be able to open it. That's what I'm saying. It's best to be congenial.
They tell me the meek -- from the Bible -- said the meek will inherit the earth. So there ain't no use of being a prima donna right away. Okay.
Now, it is too bad, because he's got a lot of talent, but there's no question that he upset people unnecessarily.

I'm going to -- y @h, Stanley, may I say something to you? Charlie Parker was one of the greatest guys on an instrument. And Birdland was named after him. They'd call him Bird, Yardbird, you see. So they named Birdland after him. We all worked downtown, and Charlie would come in late some nights. Some nights he wouldn't show. And he had a contract like $1,750.00 a week for himself. And he worked for somebody else.

And one time he worked for my rhythm section, which they had to get paid double for the week. So they made two week's salary in one week. But what they had to finally do with Charlie is pro-rate his contract. The nights he didn't show, he didn't get paid. So that -- then, fine, if he showed, okay, you get paid. If you don't show -- but when they started pro-rating his contract, he showed immediately, if not sooner. See the difference?
Yeah.

Right. So this is a source of punishment due to -- like I told you, I got (inaudible). But when he wasn't showing, they were still giving him his money because he was Yardbird. Then they started to take it out of his salary when he didn't show, he didn't like that. So that made
him show a little more often than he was doing. Always a way to ship the mule, isn't it?
(Laughter and simultaneous remarks)
I'm with you now, Mr. Dance.
They had a lot of trouble with him (inaudible).
Quite a bit.
But now then -- oh, what about -- what about Fred Beckett? What happened to him after he left that band? Did he die?

Yeah, he's dead now. Fred Beckett was a man that would wake up in the morning, and the first thing he had to have was a drink. Wouldn't eat. And he flew around and contracted tuberculosis. And they put him in the hospital in New York there, and they let him out on a pass. And he come to the theater where we were working --
(Side 7)

-- came by the Parlor, and his old girlfriend ignored him because of his situation, and that hurt him more than anything in the world. And he said, I can't understand it. They wouldn't let me out on a pass if I was contagious. And he had a weekend pass from the hospital. And he just got carried away and started to drinking and overstayed his time. When he went in the hospital, they put him out. So he went on the to St. Louis where his mother was,

and he died in St. Louis. That's the truth. He was so hurt. He should have been back in that Sunday evening. He stayed. He was there Monday, drinking. Went back to the hospital and took some half pints with him, and they put him out. They caught him with it, and he overstayed his time too. That's too much.
In other words, they were saying to him, I can't help you if you don't help yourself. That's what they were saying to him. And it was too bad.
How old would he have been, '40s?

Oh, Fred Beckett must have been -- no, he was in his '30s maybe because, see, I was in my '20s, and Fred wasn't no more than three or four years older than me. And I was 24 years old when I joined Hamp.
But did Hamp feature him much or not?
Quite a bit.
Oh, he did?
Fred Beckett played a solo before Ruby Blake come out and sing this tune titled Nightingale. You remember the thing?
Yeah.

And he put a (inaudible) and take a rubber plunger and play nothing but straight melody. Wa-wa-wa-wa-wa-wa-wa-wa-wa-wa-wa, and make chills go up and down your spine, just no nothing but melody, just improvising. But

he had that much soul. He was a soulful man, and not too many people could take a melody other than a Johnny Hudges, and Johnny Hodges was known for this. And his tone, Fred Beckett was the same thing (inaudible).
Especially with a plunger.
Huh?
Especially with a plunger.
But he put a mute.
Oh, I see, a mute.
And got in the microphone. We're at the Strand Theater.
That's like Duke's guys --
And take the wa-wa with the mute on the inside of that microphone, and I'm telling you it just makes you bloom.
There was another guy up there who disappeared. Duke Garrett. Was he there?
Duke was in San Francisco. He visited me in Houston here about three months ago.
Well, what does he do?
Duke was a trumpet player.
But what's he do now?
I don't know.
I thought he went back to the Navy or something.
No, he's not in the Navy.
No?
No.
Well, he was --

He come out of the Navy to join Hamp's band. I'd like to give you the situation on that, since you brought it up, and I was a go between man and didn't even know it. I'm always a victim of something and don't know why. Duke Garrett's brother in law was the president of the Negro Associated Press in Louisville, Kentucky, married to Duke's sister, and he asked Duke -- before he come out of the Navy, he said, what would you like to do. He said, I'd like to see you go back and finish your schooling. He said, I want to join Lionel Hampton's band.

He said, Duke, you sure you don't want to go to school? I want to join Lionel Hampton's band. Okay. Well, he talked to Hamp (inaudible) free publicity, put all the Black newspapers over the country, and Hamp's gullible for this sort of thing, you know, and he said -- you can't buy this with money (inaudible), you know.

So I'm the strawboss of the band, and Duke's been my buddy for (inaudible) me different places. He come up to (inaudible) and say hi. So he comes straight to New York. He was supposed to come to me. This is a setup, and Hamp pulls it, and I know nothing about it, but Hamp know everything.

We closed on Thursday night, and Duke got there before the last show, and I saw -- I said, wait, man. I'll see you when I come out. (Inaudible). Come out of the show, and he tells me he want to meet Hamp. Hamp already know he's coming. I don't know. Duke say, I don't need no money. I got plenty of money. He said, all I need to do is meet Lionel Hampton. I got my card here if you want to use it, whatever you want to do. He's talking to me.

Drove straight from New Orleans on the discharge. So when Hamp's coming off the stage, I'm standing on the step. I said, Hamp, I want you to meet a friend of mine. This is Duke Garrett. I said, he's from Louisville, Kentucky, just got (inaudible). He's a trumpet player. (Inaudible). He says, you got your horn with you? He said yeah. He said, meet me over to Small's. I want to hear you play. He says, okay (inaudible).

And I see Hamp, and Hamp says to me, says, who is that guy. He look like a professor or something. I still don't know. So Duke carried me home. I got my uniforms and everything. He carried me home up (inaudible) 98 West -- 159th Street (inaudible). I said, no, I'm going on and I'm going to rest. Now, he went on over to Small's.
Now, we're getting ready to go downtown and open up at the Aquarium. Duke comes and pick me up. When we get into the Aquarium, Hamp sent him around the corner to
Manning's Music Store to get him a couple of (inaudible) Boy Meets the Horn, Cootie Williams, Duke Ellington, and Duke was a (inaudible) and Duke was a (inaudible) trumpet player.
Rex Stewart.

Rex Stewart, okay, I'm sorry. And he tried to (inaudible) rehearsal, said, good. The next thing I know Dave Page got his notice. And I was blamed for it because Duke is hanging out with me. And we get in the station, train station, and Charlie Fulton. They were with Basie (inaudible). He's whispering about me, how dirty I was, what I did to Dave Page, and I don't know nothing.

But when this thing got to going so far, and what I tell you with the Curly Hammonds and the Versewis Harrison and Leroy the Ballet, and they all got real gangsterized over there, I says, time to leave.
When I left to form my band, the first man I had on trumpet was Dave Page.

No.

Well, let's get back to the record first, STANLEY (Inaudible). I had -- I didn't have a title to "Dutch Kitchen BOUNCE." I didn't have a title to Go, Red, Go. And I was almost -- you know, I was feeling sorry for him, and I was in

Oh, that's what --
That's how it come about.

No, he didn't get anything. He didn't want anything. All he wanted -- they're going to play it on the campus.
Yeah.

And he wanted the prestige in it. That's what he wanted. And I followed that, and I thought BOUGHT that. And that's where I drew the line. I went along with Bob on what he wanted, but when he wanted some lyrics and put Sarah Vaughan on it, good, but let me still control it with Wayne Music Publishing Company. That's mine. But he wanted Mills or somebody downtown in New York. No way. No way. I've been ripped off too much, and I'm tired of being ripped off. I'd take it and let it die before I'd let somebody make more money off of my own material than I could make off of it, and that's what they're going to do to me.
Why do you think he wanted to have that moved to Mills? How What would that benefit him?
Don't ask me because I don't know what people are talking behind my back.
(Inaudible) amount of money they're going to spend to push it. They're going to take it as merchandise and work on it. (inaudible) that money
And I have no control of keeping of accounting -- I was being sold on it. And they make the money.
Yeah, well, now, you've said that your back was troubling you. Is this still the back from when you were hit by the -- all this time it was --
Well, I got another blow in New York to really captivate that thing in '46 Christmas. Eddie Barfield, and I didn't tell him until I was in New York (inaudible) --

was working at NBC as a man that go on all the shows and if he had to transpose to play this instrument, then he would -- he's a utility man you'd (inaudible) and he was off during the Christmas holidays. And I had been at the Braddock Bar, and I knew that 15 minutes was going in, so I left ten minutes prior because I said (inaudible) already.

And I'm going backstage to the Apollo Theater in the snow during the Christmas holidays, and he tipped up behind me and hit me on my back with his fist. I was gasping for wind. I'm telling you, I couldn't breathe. And this time I opened the number, Airmail Special, if you remember this. I'm gasping for breath, and I couldn't hardly play the first tune. It took me a long time to get (out inaudible), and I never told him nothing about it until just this last week.

C., to supplement my band, and augment it, the (inaudible), and I never told you nothing about it because wasn't nothing you could do about it after it happened, but I don't allow nobody to talk to me with their hands anymore, because that was a lot of damage was done to me."
Did he hit you hard?
He hit me, man, with his fists.
But it was a joke, though.
He was playing, joke drunk.
: But you --
And I can't hear him coming behind me in the snow. He's tipping behind me in the snow and hit me and catch me by surprise, and I couldn't breathe on that first number, playing.
: Yeah, but he, of course, he's --
And that cost me a lot of money, playing, and cost me something to my health too.
: He was a strong --

He was a bull. Him and Ben Webster and Ben Carter wasn't nothing but football players. Them are the strongest saxophone players I know to sit up and manhandle the horn and wasn't on the field hitting somebody block and tackle. They were brutes, that's what they were. And now, he's drunk and playing with me.

And I told him. And he felt so bad. I said, I don't want you to feel bad. I've lived through it many a year now. But now I think I can tell you. You are responsible for me having that operation because you knocked the hell out of me, playing. That's the whole thing. But don't you know I held it all these years? I told him last week (inaudible). Wasn't that beautiful? What could he have done if I had told him? Nothing. He couldn't correct it. He couldn't do nothing that the doctor couldn't do. And the doctor was the one I had to go to and have the operation.
: There was a problem there before?
Pott's disease.
: Yes.

Pott's disease came from a lick. Well, I already suffered with my back, I told you, from when I got hit by the car coming out of the theater and running back, and couldn't see (inaudible) and run into the traffic, and the man hit me. All right, I suffered through the years on that. And he come and hit me later. He just added fuel to the fire to make it flame more. And that's what happened.

I don't have anything.

They're all gone now.
: I'll get some.
Got some in there? Look at the left of the stove, and you'll see on the box back there.
: Well, when you went in the first time and had the operation, and how long was that?

First time? I went in March 1st, 1948, March 1st, 1948, and I stayed in the hospital, oh, two and a half months, and I come home in a hospital bed and stayed. And I rented a hospital bed, and I stayed in it, and all together it was four months, they said. But the first doctor

gave me no antibiotics, never had any. So infection set in somewhere because I never felt right. Two months of convalescent period I went up to Greenwood Lake. I think I talked about this yesterday. And I didn't feel right.
But what did they have to do in this operation?
They went into my back and made bone replacement. A bone decayed.
Oh, I see.

They thought -- and the first time that they had to take something from a bone from my hip to transplant in there, but they didn't have to do it the first time, but the second time they took a piece of bone from here and put in there and made a fusion. They had to fuse it.

In other words, what happened, I could have laid two years without an operation but stayed quiet, and it would have stopped decaying and healed itself up. But with an operation you can get up faster, supposedly. That's what it was explained to me. So naturally, I wanted to take the fastest route.
Yes. Actually it didn't (inaudible) so much then.
It didn't. And I stayed out two and a half years.
How much were you covered by
insurance?

I was covered pretty well. I had good insurance until they just stopped. But I didn't have to pay anything out of my pocket for anything. The biggest money I spent was to live at home, with expenses going on. Really, I didn't have to pay any hospital bills. I had enough coverage there.
Thank God for that.
Well. Eelen, I wrote insurance, I told you, for Atlanta Life.
Oh, yeah.

And I knew the value of insurance. When a young man died, going to join Cootie Williams, then I became really insurance conscious for myself, you know. So I wanted enough coverage, and I'd get it for my family. I got it now. Now, I go in the hospital today and come out with money instead of paying money because I got a rider that pay me cash money that -- I bought that too.
My daughter can do the same thing. And this is an investment.
Oh, sure.
It's an investment.
(Inaudible). This is a sort of silly question that to ask you (inaudible), so, okay, you've got to lie there and all this time there's a sort of (inaudible) frustration and every-

No?
Just the idea of having to lay in bed, be turned and rubbed down and not get bedsores and this sort of thing.
Sort of the helplessness of it.

Right. I, you know, your pain is mostly two or three days after the operation, and they give you something to relieve that. And I didn't want a lot of dope. If I could take it myself, I took as much as I could take, but after that I didn't have any pain.
So it was really... healing.

Yeah, just a matter of time limit of laying. I was comfortable, and as long as I got the treatment, why they turned me over and rubbed my back and powder me down, pat me on the behind. These are things I needed for self consolation. And I got that. I got that.

So (inaudible) IN A WAY You come out of the first operation. You get ready to start (WORKING), but then you have to go in for the second, which we talked about yesterday. So now when you've got (inaudible) through the second, now what happens?
I recover from (inaudible) on the second operation?
Well, after you've had this long
period in bed after the second operation --
Well --

-- I come out for convalescing. He tested my spine with his thumb going down to see if I felt any pain, and I don't feel it.

So he gave me to lay on my stomach, to flex my back and raise up (inaudible) as hard as I could every hour on the hour. He gave me muscle situations for my legs, and I did this religiously. When I got up, I had one day on the walker, one day. And second day they put me on the crutches, and that's how he got me prepared. Seven weeks -- I didn't even know I'd been in bed.
But without the exercises to build my muscles up before I come to the hospital --
He was a wonderful doctor, wasn't he?
He -- well, he was President Roosevelt's doctor.
How do you spell his name?
Mayer, M-a-y-e-r.
M-a-y-e-r, Dr. Leo B. Mayer. I don't know if he's living or dead today.
: He must have taken a real interest in you.

He did after he met me, but I had to go through somebody, and I owed him $1,500.00, and I went to him after he let me go back to work with a walking cast on. I BROUGHT $500. (Inaudible) when I talked to him, he said, 'I told you, when I get you back on your feet, then you start to paying me.' He wouldn't accept the $500.00. He was a humanitarian as well The fellow's a doctor.
And, you know, some doctors are greedy.
: Oh, sure.

He didn't want the money really. And $1,500.00 is all I owed him for all the time that he treated me and come to my house, and I went to his office afterwards. That's all that man -- and hospital costs. Don't you know doctors all that time will charge you more money? This man was beautiful.
: Well, that must have been a great consolation.
It was. His wife dropped dead on the streets of New York with a heart attack, and I'm still under him during this time, but I'm still in bed. I hadn't gotten

up then. And by the time I got up then to go to his office, he was courting. And I was supposed to go in one day, and I was late. And he was mad as hell at me. So he went to the barbershop and got a haircut --
(Side 10)

No, but --

because otherwise it doesn't make (inaudible) what?

What, Dr. Mayer was courting?
Yeah, just (inaudible) -- FINISH UP
He had him a gal -- you know, you need --

when I went to him, he was 76 years old. And but beautiful 76, was spry and could walk fast and do everything he want to do, well kept.
