And now you -- so now when you're finished with him, you form another band.
Yeah.
And who do you get for that?

Well, on that first time I got everybody back, but the second time I did not because Charlie Forbes had gone with Basie, and he stayed there. Bootie didn't come back. I got Dickie Harris Arriage. George Rhodes Rule came back. I had another bass player, another drummer, Al Jones out of Philadelphia. And I kind of thing, trying to think -- oh, James Mosely -- Mobley on bass.
Was he any relation to Hank Mobley?
I don't know. I don't think so. But I had a good band together. Eddy Lewis on trumpet --
Oh, that's not the (inaudible).
Well, before Eddy Lewis I had Lamar Wright, Jr.
That's not Ed Lewis that was replacing--
No, no, no.
No.
Lamar Wright, Jr., first. I come out, and the first job I had was with Dinah Washington in New York on a package show, and then we went to Newark, New Jersey,
with the package show and added to it with James Moody, Dinah Washington and Arnett Cobb. We had two bands.
Who was booking you then?
Universal.
Had -- was Ben Varco alive? Barth still

Yeah. See, Ben didn't die until I come back to Houston. He died in 1966. I come back to Houston in '59. Ben dropped dead on the golf course in Miami, and Jack, his son, was walking with him when he died. See, they had a boat house down there in Miami, and Maxine and he lived -- spent a lot of time down there, and then he had trained for the office and Jack (inaudible) Jack had taken over mostly. When Ben go in, on what to do he'd give him instructions (inaudible), but he was more or less retired.

But what happened to Ben, James Brown didn't [resign] that contract, and he made a lot of money off of James. See, I brought James Brown to him. He asked me to screen him out in Georgia. Clint was his manager, the guy that had brought us for the show, package show. I was with the Five Royals at the time.

And Ben said, "I want you to put him on and tell me what you think about him." This is Macon, Georgia. Well now, we had intermission, and I come back and open up the Five Royals. [Don Eddy] closed the first half of the show. So I played one tune and brought James Brown and the Five Flings

up. And it's local, and all the house went wild. And he pleaded all over the bandstand -- "Please, please blow that thing, man." So when I called Ben and talked to him, he said, what did you think about him? I said, "Well, the leader of the group, James Brown, is good. The rest of them are a little stiff." But, I said, "They work together, what they do, the local yokel here, you know. And naturally everybody go for him. But he has the personality, and I think he got something going."

So he sent and got him. And he's put a lot of money out behind him. He bought him transportation, uniforms, hired a guy how to teach him how to get on the stand and off and put -- he ended up spending about $25,000.00. So I mean that's all along, you know.

We left here in '58 going to California on a tour, and we played the Fillmore Auditorium in San Francisco on Easter Sunday with James Brown, Leslie Hawkins -- who is getting big now -- Arnett Cobb, band backing them up, and Little Willie Johns. And you could throw a brick in the place and it wouldn't hit nobody -- on Easter Sunday. Well, they had 200 people in there, but the place was big, and they're scattered, and you can't tell how many.
How come they didn't draw?
I don't know.
James Brown?
Well, he just started. He didn't have nothing out there. Oh, that's just the beginning I'm talking about.
Oh, I see.

And I've got the master contract, and I'm receiving the money and I'm paying everybody off. We leave there and we've got one nighters to do, and we're in San Francisco at the Booker T. Washington HOTEL and got the rainy roads to Royals worry about each day -- what about during the week, blocked off on account of flooded out.
I had to send to the office and get money to bail everybody out of the hotel. That's the truth. And I just couldn't take no more. That was my second trip to California from coast to coast.
That was --
I disbanded in 1959, February, and my last job, when I made up my mind I was going to make it back to Houston and disbanded my band was in Philadelphia at the Peps Gapps Bar. I was through with it.
Well, Arnett, let me ask you something. When you got out of the hospital and started again for Universal, what year was that?
19 --wait a minute now -- '48 or '49, 1950.
So for eight years you were on the road with your own band?
Oh, yeah.
For Universal?
Until I had my accident.
When was that?
1956, April 23rd, coming out of --
How did that happen?
All righty -- let me first tell you how I got there. My wife and I were sitting up back on Friday night. She called me Hoss -- that's another one of my nicknames.
Horse?

Hoss, H-o-s-s. I told you I had many. She said, 'Hoss, let's go to Providence.' I said, 'Good,' because I heard there was something up there in the Celebrity Club, and we had friends up there, Donald and Madeline Griffith, and we called them up and, see, just like that, I made up my mind, and 6:30 the next morning we was up having coffee, getting ready to take off. I just bought this new car, first '56 Desoto push button. Remember the push button? And I called it -- I bought it for my Dungaree Doll, my daughter. She was -- when we had the accident, she was three months and 12 days old.
And we went on up to Providence and I went into the

Celebrity Club on a Saturday night, and I was getting ready to regroup my band FOR a little more entertainment, not just and I just musicianship -- (inaudible) everybody's great but nobody's entertaining. I'm getting ready to get what I want to get to have a little more life in the group. I spotted what I wanted to spotted and I told the guys, said, "I'll call you on Tuesday and let you know when to come down, and I'll have a rehearsal." (inaudible).

So I said to Griff -- who we were staying with. This is Madeline and Donald. "I'm leaving Sunday." He said, "Why don't you stay until Monday? You ain't got nothing to do." Well, I said, "I promised Ben Barth I was going to stop back through New Rochelle and see him on Sunday. That's my agent." He said, "Do you have to?" Well, I said, "I can call him and let him know I'll be in Monday, and I'll call him at the office on Monday." And he said, "Why don't you do that, just stay over? We hate to see you all leave."

So I did. I called Ben. I told him, said, "I'm not coming in today. I'll call you at the office," I said, (inaudible) whatever you've got at the office, (inaudible), and I told him what progress I'd made and what I found and what I intended to do. He said, "good."

I left out Monday morning at 10:00 o'clock and got into Hartford around 12:00. We had lunch there. And I asked my wife, I said, "How do you feel about driving?" I don't know, maybe a premonition. She said, "I've got a headache," and said,

Rosetta will be waking up in a few minutes, and I'm going to have to feed her. So go on and drive, I said OK. (inaudible). 16 miles south of Hartford, little town called Meridian had the staggering system of lights, and I just cruised. And I got to the -- just almost to the last light and swallowed my own saliva, and it hit my windpipe, and I gave a cough to kick it out and blacked out, driving.
Oh?

I ended up in a filling station yard and hit a tree dead on center, missed the pumps, thank God. And the motor, you know, down and went under the car instead of coming back in on my wife and me. My baby was in the top of the chassis that Ben had given us for a buggy, and we had the bottom of it in the trunk of the car. And that tilted over and hit the seat, and then by (inaudible) one of those steel was on it because (inaudible) like this she got a bump on the forehead that kept her 48 hours under observation, (inaudible). That girl in there.

And my mother took her down to New York. She come and picked her up and took her. Wasn't nothing wrong with her, nothing but just a little bump, and she was screaming and carrying on, and she was groanin.' (inaudible) I couldn't move my legs and -- a doctor, tourist doctor passing by stopped and told me keep my head back. I was bleeding at the mouth. I'd hit something. And you can he could see the scar here where I hit. I could take my tongue through my top lip and bottom lip, and

I must have hit the horn rim on the impact with my head going FORWARD. (inaudible). I had a fusion on this hip, and it's solid and that's why most of the damage was to this leg. This didn't give way, and my back didn't give where I had the fusion, solid as a rock, but it took the damage THERE. I had three clean breaks (inaudible).
How fast a rate were you going?

I couldn't tell you because I was just only 3 miles from the Merritt Parkway. (inaudible) So I couldn't tell you how fast, but it was hard enough. (Inaudible). Brand new -- I'm going in for the 5,000 mile checkup.
Was your wife hurt?
Oh, yeah. That was part of her death, from that accident. She lived from '56 to '70.
What happened to her then?

Well, both of her lungs collapsed, and they had to give her pneumotherapy, build her lungs up, and this is what happened with her. It was a lung condition. She had a hemorrhage. Just a cough -- she gave a cough and spat up blood about the size of a quarter, hit the runner in our place out there on Peacock. And she said heu-eu-um. Thomas Joe Cormoth was supposed to come in the next day to go Beaumont for a funeral, and my wife had talked to Laverne that evening about 5:00 o'clock, cooking dinner. And she said, "Joe'll be in tomorrow," which was on a Friday. This is
whose birthday February 12th, 1970, on (inaudible). Was that on the 12th of February?
I think Washington --

Lincoln -- one of them, yeah. And she said, 'Well, we could take him.' And she said, because she didn't want Joe to try to get a rent a car and drive because he had his condition of diabetes and heart condition and she'd rather not trust him to drive, you know. So she told us the flight number and what time he'd be in, and we said we'd pick him up and we'd take him (inaudible). He'd stay with us tonight, and we'd take him tomorrow.

So after we hung up that night later on my wife called the house here, where my mother and her mother was living right here, and her mother'd gone to bed, and she talked to my mother, and said, 'Grandma,' said, 'Let me talk to mother.' She's asleep. Well, tell her to be ready at 9:00. I'm going to take her to the hairdresser and get her hair done, and we're going to Beaumont. Joe Thomas Formoth's coming in.' Blah, blah, blah, and just like that -- okay.

Nurse across the street, Marie -- she's a German girl and her husband worked at Borden and all, Borden Milk Company, and normally Rogers is a critical guy, but he sat over here this night, and Marie was teaching my wife how to crochet with needles and things, whatever, and we're looking at a movie, Roger and I together, and finally they sat and sat

and sat until about quarter to 11:00, and Roger said, "I'm hungry." Oh, Elizabeth said, "Oh, man, you can eat anytime." "No," he said, "I'm staying over here since 7:00 something." He said, "I'm hungry now." So they left and went home.

So she come to me, and she said, "You hungry?" I said not really. She said, "How would you like a piece of buttered toast?" I said, "That sounds good." She went and made the buttered toast, and I'm still looking at the movie. She said, "Did you find out who did it yet?" You know, whatever the crime was. I said, "Not yet."

She come in with me, and we sat down and we ate our toast together. We had twin chairs with a table (inaudible). She said, "I feel -- Hoss, I feel like I want another piece. You want another piece?" I said no. She went to fix her another piece of toast. As she stood, asked me, being away from the television, catching me -- find out who it was? I said, "No, not yet."

And she come back in and was looking -- and all of a sudden she gave a cough. She had a white rug in the living room, and it had a plastic runner, and she coughed and a spot of blood about the size of a quarter, and she said, huh-uh-uh. I looked at her, and she wheeled and went in the bathroom. And I got up (inaudible). When I got in the bathroom, just like she turned the faucet on. Blood was everywhere. She hemorrhaged.
Well, how long after the accident was this?
Huh?
How long after the accident was this?
Well, the accident was in '56. She died in '70.
You mean that's when she died?
I mean she died like this, with the hemorrhage?

Oh, she died -- she was dead before she left the house, but they didn't let me know. And they rushed her out of there and put her in the car. I'd gone in the garage and opened the tailgate to my station wagon for to lay her down in it. I finally got Marie to come over, and Marie's a nurse, so I could get to the doctor. And the doctor said, 'Meet me at the hospital.' And Marie talked to her.
And this was a result of that accident?
Oh, yeah, had to be. It was acute pulmonary hemorrhage. And it comes from weakness of the lungs.
Had -- had she felt all right?
She was feeling good all day, but just one

of those things that happens, and I called Laverne back in Kansas City, and had to tell them that Elizabeth was dead. And Joe was coming to a double funeral. Laverne said, "Don't to Elizabeth today, kid with me. I talked a little, and hung up on me. Then she called me back in an hour, about an hour later. I had called my mother and everything.

My daughter went into a tangent. She was in the room studying for a test the next day. She didn't know what happened. She don't know when they took her mother out. All she knew, she come out and went in the bathroom and saw all this blood, said, "What happened?" I said, Mommy had a hemorrhage." She said, "Will Mommy be all right?" I said, "God knows I hope so."

And we had finished talking about five minutes. Dr. Jones called me. She said, "Arnett?" I said, "Yes, Dr. Jones." And the phone went dead. I knew it had happened. She waited for a while. She said, Elizabeth is dead." I couldn't say nothing.
When you had this blackout, it was due to coughing?

So, he said, got a pair of shoes and sent it out, and he had built up for me because I'm getting ready to go. (inaudible). But they didn't do it in cork, they did it in leather, and that was a heavy shoe, and, oh, my God, I thought I was lifting a ton.
But I finally found out about the cork and all my shoes are done in cork now, and it's lighter.

Beautiful, yeah, beautiful.

We did a lot of battling traveling too, and we did -- I did recordings with Eddy, you know, (inaudible) one "Where or When," of the things here with me on (inaudible), but it was a beautiful tour, and we played one head arrangement. That was ("Jumpin' with Symphony Sid" -- ed.) the opening. La-de-doo-day-day-deedle-day-doo-dee, yo-dee, and Milton Buckner would call -- he was the man in charge and the leader of the group, and they was jumping from wherever you were, jumping for Bardot, jumping for Paris, jumping for whatever you are. This is especially for you-all, you know?
Yeah.
Only that was the warm-up. Everything else (inaudible), but it was a beautiful tune, beautiful.

Well, you know, it's a funny thing, isn't it, that -- I mean this guy has done these tours, and everybody else has sort of taken the same old names back year after year, same people go year after year, and he keeps taking
all kinds of people like that. I mean they'd never heard of Candy Johnson until he took him.

Yeah, well, Candy'd been around. He used to be with the old Andy Kirk band. He was with Bill Doggett after the Scotty (inaudible) left. He's been around for a while, but he's mainly stationed in Toledo. He teaches school there, and his wife does too, in the same school. So this year he just -- they called him on the short notice, and he paid his own way over there, and they had to reimburse him.

And he had his wife, and he was determined to find Ben Webster. For some reason or another he had to see Ben. But he could not find out where Ben was or where he went. So we got to Zurich, Switzerland, and he saw Johnny Simmons. Johnny Simmons is a writer.
Yeah, I know.

Knew everybody. Knew their whereabouts, and he told him where Ben Webster was, in Denmark. Gave him his phone number and everything. And he called him from Zurich, from Zurich. He said, 'I just want to know if you were there.' Now (inaudible) he just -- all he want to do, because he loved Ben Webster. He put his wife on a plane to go back to the States, and he went up there and stayed four days.
Now (inaudible) he wrote a letter saying about his situation. He enjoyed Dexter Gordon coming to town. They had

a party at Dexter's house, and they jammed for four days together at different clubs, and two weeks later Ben's dead, two weeks later. And there's -- so that's why I say, he must have had a premonition because he was determined. He was asking everybody about Ben Webster, Ben -- he said, 'I've got to see him while I'm on this trip, while I'm over here.' And good thing he did see him, because if he'd left and didn't see him, he never would have seen him anymore anyway.
Somebody told me -- I think it was John [Ralby] told me that while you were over there (inaudible) you had to go somewhere about 200 miles on a bus or something, and you had to stand all the way.
Who?
You.
I didn't stand nowhere. No, indeedy.
They said something --
I don't know how John got hold of that.
Some sort of story. He said that you never complained, that you --
Well, I ride maybe 200 miles without -- I don't complaining about anything. It's no sense complaining when you can't do anything about it. But I didn't stand up no 200 miles.
What kind of traveling is a Monestia able to lay on? Is --
They have a bus sort of a type vehicle. They've got a new one now, but with reclining seats. It's very comfortable. Yeah, very comfortable. And I'm a bus rider, not the car rider.
Oh, really?
Because the ones that drive the car are crazy as hell, and they go too fast for me.
And after what you've been through.
I don't want that. That's the big one, Jean-Pierre. He loves to drive fast.
(Inaudible) Jean-Pierre --
And all of a sudden, stop the brakes on a dime and -- shut you down like this.
They don't make -- the jumps are not too far, huh?

Some of them, but we'd never -- we never travel -- only one time we traveled at night. We don't do it at night because we stay overnight everywhere we go. You do sleep, if you don't sleep but four hours in a hotel room. So we put up. Yeah, we put up. No night traveling.
How are you doing?
Well, this is hard to see, so I'm going to just watch it now. All right, now the next time you go is to -- you come up for Newport then east. Is that right?
This year?
Well --
Or last year?

Yeah, went to New York and played Roseland Ballroom, and I played with Sy Oliver's band, On the package like it was Basie's band -- Joe Williams; Barney Bigard was over on our side of the fence and Sy. This was a good -- kept everybody on the dancing side.
Yeah, I know.
Danceable music --
I'm sure you did. But then you went to Nice and you got --
We left the next day going to Nice.
And that was where you had really a big triumph? Yeah, we can say that without being immodest because it's a fact, isn't it?
If you say so.
Well, that night at the Roseland was a triumph too.
Huh?
That night at the Roseland was a triumph for you too.
It was, yes.
It's not me who says so. It's
everybody says so.
George Wein

John Williams comes to Nice and tells everybody, said, 'This man come all the way from Texas and broke it up.' I said, 'Broke what up?' He said, 'Man, you was the star of the show.' I said, 'I wasn't.'
(Laughter)
I didn't do nothing but what I did when I left Houston and what I'd done in Houston, I'm and was doing the same thing I'd been doing all my life. And that's all I could do, you know.
Now, this --
It's nice when people think --
Oh, well, sure it is.
I like that.
Then this year you're going to do it again, are you?

Yes, going back with Lionel, (inaudible). We're leaving on the 29th of April. We (rehearse) (inaudible) on the 30th of June -- I mean -- 29th of April -- 29th of June and rehearse on the 30th of June and the first of July. We play a concert at Carnegie Hall on the first, that night, of July. We go to Saratoga on the 2nd, and we're off on the third and leave on the 4th, get into Nice on the 5th. We have --
(Side 12)
Pretty well.
So, yeah, you recently played a
concert in Boston, a tribute to Lionel -- to Lionel Hampton.
Yeah, we did that on the 15th of this month, which is March, yeah. Yeah.
And who was in that band? That was like a tryout for Nice, in a way.
Yeah, I might can't call all the names of everybody in the group or remember all the names, but I'll give you the -- rhythm section was Ray Brown on piano --
Bryant --

-- Bryant, Ray Bryant, and Major Holly, the Mule, on bass, Grady Tate on drums, Mackel, Bill Mackel, who's been with Lionel Hampton for 963 years, on guitar. And in the trumpet section I can't call all the names -- Joe Newman, Doc Cheatham. Oh, my goodness gracious me -- two more other guys.
Trombone was Janice Robinson, a gal playing trombone. You know Janice.
She played with Fletcher a plunger?
Yeah, yeah, she did.
Can she blow?
Yeah, she can blow. She's a good musician. Let me go to my reed section because I can't remember -- I'm not a (inaudible) -- (inaudible) --
Well, that isn't --
I've got to do it. Earl Warren played EARLE

first. Eddy Barefield played third alto and tenor. Ham's musical director was Paul Moen. He's been with him a couple years now. Pepper Trevor Martin on baritone and yours truly the other one more time on (inaudible) tenor and that was it.
Then you had Alan Dawson, who was extra -- Ernie Williams, who was extra, McGee, who was extra --
: Howard McGhee (Inaudible) or tenor?
No, no, no, tenor player McGee, Alan McGee or something like that.
: No, no, you (inaudible) something like that.
He works at Berklee School of Music. (Andy McGhee -- ed.)
: Right.

And we had a little gal 12 years old by the name of Terry Carrington played drums, and she gave Lionel Hampton a fit. I mean she can play. I have never heard anything like that so young in my life, the way that girl -- she played like a man and solo and even -- everything's even. When she'd get through, she said, doodle-dee-doo-doo, dooley-doo-doo-bop. You could (inaudible) say you got it now.
I mean on the beat.
: That's (inaudible) terrific because a lot of -- sometimes these kids can play solos, but --
The only thing I --
: This is a little Black girl?

Yeah. Cute as a button. The only thing I say, I think her daddy's pushing her too fast for her age to promote her because she's in school and let her finish her education. You know, you got some parents that might want to commercialize on their kid, you know, and she -- he could commercialize on her because she's got something to offer, but she need an education first. That's the only objection I have.
But you had rather a bad time traveling up there, didn't you?
I had a bad time traveling coming back in that snow, and I didn't have no snow shoes.
And who looked out for you on that --

I had a good friend from Jersey, Doc Nepples. He used to be my tenant in my house over there. He come and pick me up at the airport, took me into New York in the rain, hour late the plane was getting in, but he waited until I got there, then hung out with me, took me to Jersey and then come back and picked me up when I came back from Boston to take me to the airport.
Was he with you when they cancelled and said --
No, he had gone then because he didn't linger on account of the snow. He said, 'I better get on back to Jersey.' He saw that if I got to the airport, and I thought

I was home free, checked my bags through with the skycap, and they gave me my ticket, baggage check ticket, went on down to my gate, checked in, got my boarding ticket, and about three seconds after he gave me my board ticket, said now, on the loudspeaker, "All of you that are headed for Houston on Flight 367 will be transferred to Kennedy Airport." Oh, my God, no. Everybody rose like they was in church, and the preacher said, get up, and started to walking, back up to the steps, and I had -- we had to go to the baggage room and get our baggage to claim them, get them all out where they could ship them over.
Oh, and everybody had to carry their own bag?
No, no, you claim your bag.
Oh.
With your baggage check number.
Yeah.
To send from there to Kennedy. And they sent them by bus. I got everything when I got to Houston. Wasn't none (inaudible).
Just your horn and --
My horn and a valet pack. And I had my shoulder bag with me. I just had three pieces.
Did you check your horn through?
Yeah, I can't handle all that (inaudible) a plane.
No, how could you?

I have to trust them. But this horn I carry, very well compact in the case and it's not like my other horn that it jolts around and may be damaged when I get there, but if you take a look when I get through -- when I get through I show you how it's put in and everything's in grooves.
So it won't move.
Yeah, it won't move. And that's an asset, you know.
All right, Arnett, now we're nearly up to date. What are those other things you've got for me?

Well, I wanted to let you know when I was working at the Zanzibar in New York at 49th and Broadway -- they had a guy from the Daily News that was a critic. I can't think of Bob's last name. Maybe you would know who he was, the musical critic for the Daily News.

No, this was in the '50s, early '50s. But anyhow, I had six pieces with Bootie, me and Dave Page. Rhythm section was Joe Harris. Bass player -- what was his name? Walter Buchanan. And the piano player was George Phil Joey Rhodes. Of course, here I am again, six pieces. But he said it sounded like a mob, six pieces. And we're working opposite of Barnet, Charlie Barnet. And Charlie would come on and play,

and then we'd come on and play, and he said, you sound like a mob. So he gave me the name Arnett Cobb and the Mobb -- (Laughter) -- spelled with two Bs, M-o-b-b. And he was the one that was instrumental in getting me in Birdland.

But on this particular date Charlie Barnet went up there to talk to California, and he had some -- what them long necked things, birds, long neck -- ostriches? He had some and somebody (inaudible) he talked to his old lady, and they were getting along bad. He was having domestic trouble, and he come down on the bandstand on his next (inaudible) set and took his soprano saxophone and took it across his leg and bent it and told everybody, "I'm through with the music business" and threw it on the floor and walked back out.
I said I don't believe this. He's stone millionaire. He can buy another tomorrow. But I ain't going be that crazy to break mine over my leg. Nothing --
(Simultaneous remarks)
I'm just going back into business from my operation, you know, and things.
Well, I hope to fit that in here.
But it was the latter part, but he was instrumental -- he said, "You should be down in Birdland." So

I went to Birdland, and I had a graduated contract. I started with so much money a week, and each time I'd go back and get another $100.00 increase over a period of time. So I finally got in there now on one occasion. I'd played opposite many musicians, Dizzy Gillespie, (inaudible) Charlie Parker. I told you he used my rhythm section in there.

But I went in there one time with Willis Jackson, and George Rhodes was writing for me. Reuben Phillips was writing for me, and they keep the scores, and they was giving Willis same arrangement, and I'm trying to miss him, and he's trying to miss me without playing the same thing. I got so mad, boy, and George was with me on bass. I said, 'Man, you ought to be shame of yourself to make more money off the same arrangement you wrote for' -- I'm not lying to you.
Well, that's very unethical.

And not -- we got to figure how we can miss one another and we won't get on the stand and play the same thing over. And they did that to me. And George did (inaudible) too. They kept the scores and just copied off for another band.
Well, that's very unusual, isn't it?
Well, they figured we'd never cross paths, but here we're working together, and when one come off, the other one goes on.
Oh, I see.
How in the hell you going to get by with after that. Something Willis that? I had to go and tap dance out there. That some Jackson wasn't doing, dancing, really (inaudible), tap dancceer.
Now, they've done this before the two of you went in together.
Huh?
They'd given you these arrangements, not knowing that the two of you would be playing opposite one another?
That was the general idea, but we met on this occasion, and George is up there, one of the guilty parties, playing piano for me.
Well, I mean and Duvivier did (inaudible) played the same thing?
I'm telling you -- had the same -- I couldn't believe it. I said, 'Hell, he's playing the same thing I'm about to play.'
(Laughter)

I was (inaudible). I was so mad, and I got provoked, and, you know, I don't usually get provoked. I'm a pretty good guy, but I turned redder than a beet in the face there and I'm ready to cuss everybody out. And I'm fighting playing this, and I got to go back and think what the hell I can do. And I can't talk to Willis because when I'm on, he's off. When he's off, I'm on. How you going to talk to him? You don't have time to say nothing.
Just listen to what he play.
(Laughter)
In the next set try to beat him to it. That's all you can do.
You must have --
But, man, I had a miserable two weeks in there with that.
And two whole weeks?
Two weeks.
You should have made those guys (inaudible) sit down and write arrangements every night.
(Simultaneous remarks)
I go in like two weeks at a time in there, you know, and I'm telling you.
(Inaudible). That is awful, isn't it?

The only thing George Now didn't do for him was the Ellington medley, and he couldn't do it for him because the way it was, Willis couldn't have done it because he didn't have the same instrumentation I had for what I was going to do. Oh, my God. That is miserable.
Yeah, that's --
Those guys must have been very embarrassed, weren't they?
(Inaudible) God bless Reuben Phillips, so -- he's dead now, but I had to tell him. I told George

Duvivier (inaudible), I said, "Man, anytime you make another arrangement for me, give me the score. Now, if I got to pay for it, give me the whole works because I don't want nobody else playing the same thing I'm playing. I don't want to run into this hassle anymore." (inaudible).
It's ridiculous.
Sure, it's ridiculous.
I'm surprised George, you know, George is usually (inaudible).
Man, they were making money. That's what they was doing. Now, who else had it, I don't know. I didn't cross them. But I crossed Willis Jackson in Birdland because we played on the same bill together.
Well, what's the next item on the agenda?

Well, I'm telling you about the Billie Holiday thing. I think I talked to you about that. Then after my accident that Dinah Washington, she looked out for me. And I was in the hospital after I come back under Dr. Leo B. Mayer. She come in before the Christmas holidays, and she called me Hoss too, because that was my nickname then. She got it from me and my wife, calling one another (inaudible) Hoss. She says, "Hoss, what you got up there?" I had a little bird laying in my room, had my tape recorder, had my radio, putting my (inaudible) out the window.

She said, "Do you got anything to drink up there?" I said, "No, nothing but some beer." She said, "I'm going to send you some scotch, some bourbon, some vodka, some gin, and I'm going to send you your dinner. You got a TV up there?" I said no. She said, "I'm going to send you a TV." She sent all this to me.
Wasn't that wonderful.

I spent my Christmas of 1956 in the Hospital for Joint Disease at 124th and Madison, and all the nurses visited me, and I gave them a drink for Christmas. They come in my room and hide and smoke. I had me a little old buddy in there from Chicago, but he got out (inaudible) wasn't but two in the room. He got out and left, and they left me by myself. They'd come in there and smoke their cigarettes. "You got a little drink?" Yeah, open the cabinet up. I got everything you need." I got the music going, got the tape recorder on. I'm playing the sounds.
(Laughter)

But I had fun. I got out, I told you, on the 12th of January. Dinah is opening at the Apollo Theater, and what I did, on my way home, dropped the television off by the apartment because she was opening that day I got out. Isn't that beautiful?
Terrific. That was so nice of --
But she sent me $50.00 --
: -- her.
-- and I didn't get it.
: How come?

Well, she gave it to Ann in St. Louis, and she asked me did I get it, and I said, 'No, Dinah, I didn't get it.' She said, 'I'll find out why you didn't get it because I know who I gave it to to mail to you,' and she got on big Ann's (inaudible) behind. Excuse me.
(Laughter)
I got my $50.00. I got it.
: She is a sweetheart.

Dinah was beautiful. She took care of her mother. She bought her mother a home in Chicago and bought a car for her stepdaddy, Buick, and she was a lucky girl because she was good to her mother. She was good to her mother. And her mother was the only one that she wouldn't talk back to. She'd talk back to anybody but Ms. Jones. See, Dinah's real name was Ruth Jones. But Ms. Jones would take her back hand and clap her in the mouth if she said anything, and Dinah respected that woman. I was half scared of her myself.
(Laughter)
: She had a big vocabulary. (inaudible) I know I heard her one --
I tell you one thing, she never used it with Ms. Jones.
(Laughter)
I don't care how big it was. You've never seen Dinah so meek and humble in your life until she gets to Chicago around her mother.
(Laughter)
Well, that's good.
Oh, sure, I love that respect. I love that respect. But anybody else, she'd blast off. Gladys Hampton did (inaudible) she didn't want to be there. She didn't want to hear Dinah put her mouth on.

I'll give you an incident. We're in Los Angeles, and we're working out of Southgate, California, at this club out there. And Dinah has been called on two recordings. You know, she'd never recorded with Hamp, but she'd been promised to record. And every time she get to the Decca studio, whether it was in New York or Hollywood, Hamp turned it into instrumental.

Milton Buckner on the second one had made a tune for (inaudible) Ray called "Million Dollar Smile." Da-da-da-da-da-da -- don't you remember that (inaudible). And Dinah sang the hell out of it on all the theater engagement and crack up the house. But when it got to the studio in Hollywood, Hamp decided it was going to make it a vibes five

specialists, and that girl cried a million. (inaudible). Dinah never drank nothing in her life. She went out and got her a fifth of gin that day, and she come up -- we're working at the Pea Trianon and Arm Ballroom in Southgate. Come to work that night, Hamp was sitting in the room back there where they used to have a TV or radio booth where you had a glass to look out and all this, and that was his dressing room back there.

Dinah had a dressing room upstairs. And Dinah had bought her a pistol. It didn't even have a firing pin in it. She didn't know. What she knew about a pistol was nothing. But that thing was -- if you'd have snapped it, it wouldn't have shot nothing.

She got on, and Hamp gave me up -- I'm (inaudible). the straw. set, and to end the set he had for Dinah the gave me singing He came with the first tenor player and (inaudible) The Man I Love." Instead of Dinah singing "The Man I Love," she laughed, because they were saying, "Sing it, Miss Gin," quietly, and she just laughed through it because she was high enough. Hamp wanted to know what was wrong. And he called me up in -stairs after that. audible}. I said, "I don't know."

George Jenkins was her husband. He called George. He said, "Man, I don't know about your vocalist. You talk to her. She's just my wife." Finally he called Dinah in and asked her. Gladys and Curly gone to the movie. So they got in a heated argument, Dinah and Hamp. And she (inaudible) she mad because she ain't recorded, and the least thing Hamp

said was the worst thing with Dinah right here, and Hamp don't know it. And they got in this heated argument, and finally he told her, "kiss my ass." (inaudible), and she went upstairs and got that pistol and come back down, said, you told me to kiss your ass, and put that gun right in his -- right between his nose, his eyes, over the top of his nose, and Hamp's hair turned green. I ain't never seen anybody's hair turn green.
Were you there?
Who? I'm right there. It ain't but an inch off the (inaudible).
Oh, it was right on the stand?

No, in the dressing room. You know Hamp didn't come out of that dressing room until Gladys and Curly come from the theater, and the show hadn't been on yet? Hamp wasn't coming out there. That's the scaredest man in the world. But I tell you what happened. When Gladys come and Hamp told her what happened, she terminated Dinah's contract that she had for ten years for $75.00 a week.
Oh, that was wonderful.
She had a Broadway show for $350.00 and couldn't make it.
She had her for how many years at $75.00?
Ten years for $75.00 a week, but she didn't know. If you don't know, Helen, you don't know.
But you'd have thought somebody could have caught on to that and broken that for her. But she did it for herself.
Well, she didn't try. She didn't try.
She broke it for herself right there.
She broke it with that pistol, and it wouldn't even fire.
(Laughter and simultaneous remarks)

-- I don't let nobody wreck my living, and Hamp was her living. And then Hamp begged her to go up to San Francisco for two weeks. She said, "No way. No way." I'm just telling you like it is. I was there.
But she, of course, at this time wasn't quite the big star she was going to become.
No, she got to be the star because Big Ben Barth Barr made her.
Did he?
Oh, sure. Sure. He put -- now, we did a thing. We were in the Apollo Theater for -- what the hell's the name of this record company that -- Linn --
Harry Linn,
-- and Leonard Feathers -- Keynote.
Yeah.
We did a session working in the Apollo Theater -- (inaudible) in the morning. And that's when

"Dinah did, I Know How To Do It," Salty Papa Blues." Remember this? She did four sides that morning. Milton Buckner was on that set. Even Hamp played two finger pianos on it, but he -- she couldn't record with him. Well, Hamp wanted to get in on the deal.

I made that next -- first show the next morning with one eye open, because we had to take some liquor on that date to keep our eyes open and keep happy. We recorded until 5:00 in the morning. And our (inaudible) hour was 10:30. Listen to me.
I was going to say --
(Inaudible) show went on at 11:00 o'clock.
-- (inaudible). Yeah, and five shows.

We were (inaudible) show people were standing three abreast from 7th Avenue all the way over to 8th Avenue, both sides of that theater with that band. That was the damndest band, and they did it in Philadelphia. I could name anyplace that -- in the rain with umbrellas, waiting to get in, and I'm selling the Lionel Hampton Swing Book got my wife out in the lobby, and I'm making a quarter out of every book. Shoot, I was cleaning up too.
(Laughter)
I've been hustling all my life, you know. I had to hustle to (Inaudible) would
make me a quarter. Well, you need money to live on, because I just told you I don't want a lot. I just want to be comfortable. That's all.
Got to use your wits.
Got to do it.
All right, are there some more items?
Let me see what I've got.
There isn't much tape left, (Inaudible).
Well, I told you about the Hustle Heaven and Basie wasn't Herschel Evans situation down there in Bass One down there, didn't I?
Yeah.

Told you about the Carnegie Hall situation, the Ralph Cooper situation and blah, blah, blah and about my mother. You know, after my wife died, I brought my mother out there with me, and she took care of me. But she was a woman of great understanding. And anytime I'd get depressed or have any problem, I could go to her and talk to her, and she'd always have something good to say. She was clean in thought and in heart, and never give you the wrong advice.

And, of course, I had problems in '75 with my present wife, and she walked off and left me on October the 6th, and then, of course, my mother thought everything was upset. But we was having -- lot of it was my fault. I'm drinking. I raise hell, you know, and this sort of a thing,

and she just walked because she don't like no arguments and -- can't stand it, you know. And my mother thought everything was straight and everything, so by the same token, she took sick and we were still good friends and everything. She come home and she helped me put my mother in the hospital on November 15th, got the insurance straight for her.

I'm telling you the truth. We went to see her, and she was -- had that smile. And I just went in for a checkup. I went there Thanksgiving night, and she still had that smile, Thanksgiving Eve. Went back there (inaudible) and she had another stroke, lived for (inaudible) water in her mouth and never come back anymore, and on the 17th of December she passed.

I got the call at 2:00 o'clock in the morning from the hospital, which is unusual. Then my doctor called me at 7:00 and told me she was dead, and I said, 'I know it already.' She said, 'How did you know?' I said, 'The hospital called me.' And I know she was mad because (inaudible) they aren't supposed to tell nothing the doctor said, but I had to tell her I knew it. I couldn't lie to her. I couldn't lie because I knew it, and I'm (inaudible) already. So why should I have to lie? You know, it doesn't make sense.
: No.
Broke up, I'm broke up over it, but that was one woman I could go to. I don't care how bad my problem was, she had something good to lift me up with.
And when you think she fought for you from the time you were little, when she was going to beat up the guy when you had the pleurisy, oh, yes.
She was going to kill him, not beat him up, kill him.
(Laughter)
Messing with her son -- and coming back from 170 pounds down to 119 1/2 and you can count my ribs. You know she was going kill him.
Well, it's wonderful you had her with you all your life.
I'm very grateful to have her 76 years. A lot of people don't have their mothers that long.
That's right.

Or fathers that long, but you just go with what you got while you got it. That's why I got that sign: 'God, grant me to accept change' (inaudible) the things I cannot tell you -- nothing I could do about that.
When Norma came, she didn't stay away from you then, huh?
Two years. But one morning about 2:00 o'clock she called me, after she got over her mad -- I don't know what the hell she was mad about.
Took her two years?
Yeah. She didn't want to speak to me.
You must have been acting very bad.
I must have been doing something.
You must.
But she come back, I said, "God damn it, what's on your mind?" She said, "I'm just so lonesome, and I miss you." Yes, she did tell me that. But she didn't know how glad I was to hear that.
(Laughter)
But I didn't know what to say to her. I swear to God (inaudible) because I'm a little timid. She's got more guts than I got.
But that's all right. We got guts together now.
(Laughter)
Long as there's a happy ending.
Yeah, that's the most important. You see, (inaudible) get ready to walk, October the 6th. I remember the date she walked on me.
(Simultaneous remarks)
See that little girl sitting right there? She said, "Come on, Tina, let's go." Those were her last words -- "Come on, Keemer, let's go."
You don't remember the date I found you.
(Inaudible). You still got that microphone on me?
Sure.
Smithsonian going to overcharge you.
(Laughter and simultaneous remarks)
Where is this place we're to meet you at 9:15?
Right around the corner (inaudible) Blodgett.
On Blodgett?
Blodgett is the first light. You go past it to your hotel.
There's a stop light at that corner, Blodgett and Crawford.
Blodgett and Crawford. Listen, Norma, if we come out from the hotel (inaudible) come down to like Fanon and --
Make your little circle right there.
-- make the circle.
Yeah, because you got a one way going that way coming from --
(Simultaneous remarks)
-- or this side of the Holiday Inn.
What's the name of the place?
Club [Le Bicque.] Now, I'm going to tell you. When you go to the corner here, you turn left and go up to the first light and turn right, and that's Blodgett.
That's the street we're playing on.
(Simultaneous remarks)
When you cross Almeda --
I know where it is.
When you cross Almeda, you're going to go about two or three blocks. You go look on the right hand side and pass it going to the hotel, it's like a little old shopping area inset off the street.
That's it.
And there's place to park there?
You can't miss them red doors and all that (inaudible). Club La Bicque.
Listen, how long you been playing there?
Been now over three years, three years this past December.
And who is with you there?
Kenny Andrews on organ, Ben Turner on drum, Larry Slezak on tenor and once again I got to say Yours Truly, Arnett Cobb.
Who was -- Larry --
S-l-e --
S-l-e-z-a-k.
Sounds like a Pole.
