segments.title: Copyright notices, Smithsonian header and start of taping
segments.summary: Archive copyright notices, the Smithsonian oral history title page, and the Danceses setting up the recorder before the first question on birth.

segments.title: Born in Houston in 1918; a musical family
segments.summary: Cobb gives his birth date, August 10, 1918, and says his grandmother taught piano and his mother, an uncle and an aunt played.

segments.title: His father's death and the Chesterfield overcoat
segments.summary: His father died when Cobb was six; he remembers him mainly for a gray Chesterfield coat with a fur collar and how proud he was of new clothes.

segments.title: Living in his grandfather's large household
segments.summary: Cobb lived with his grandfather, a boilermaker with ten children who ran the house by his own law and bought food in bulk; his father died of tuberculosis.

segments.title: Cheap food then and the falling dollar now
segments.summary: Cobb recalls four-cent sausage and three-cent bread, and the talk turns to the dollar being worth 26 cents and the pointlessness of saving.

segments.title: Grandfather's curfew and the uncle who was whipped and thrown out
segments.summary: A young uncle sneaks in past curfew, is whipped, leaves the house and never returns; Cobb stresses his grandfather's stern convictions.

segments.title: Elementary school and fifty violin lessons on Saturdays
segments.summary: After elementary school near home, Cobb enters Phillis Wheatley High and takes a mail-order style deal of fifty violin lessons at a downtown Houston building, getting the violin free.

segments.title: Houston in the 1930s as a country town
segments.summary: Talk of Houston as a small place then, with his mother predicting it would become a great Southern city, and where on Nance Street he lived.

segments.title: From violin to the school band and a C melody saxophone
segments.summary: Cobb is the lone violin in an 80-piece brass band, the instructor hands him a C melody saxophone with his mother's consent, and he learns it by transferring his piano and violin knowledge.

segments.title: Getting the tenor saxophone chair in the school stage band
segments.summary: When the stage band's tenor player falls ill, Cobb is pulled out of Latin class to rehearse and takes over the tenor, which he has played ever since.

segments.title: C melody versus tenor, and whether C melody has any jazz use
segments.summary: Cobb explains that moving from C melody to tenor was easy apart from the key; the Danceses ask about the C melody's sound and Kenny Davern, and he calls it a marching band horn.

segments.title: The nickname Obay, and Frankie Trumbauer
segments.summary: Friends called him Obay because C melody and oboe share a key; the Danceses mention his grandfather's nickname Rooster, and the talk touches Frankie Trumbauer.

segments.title: Buying a bass clarinet and doubling in Hampton's band
segments.summary: Cobb bought a bass clarinet for $75 from a soldier, borrowed money from Gladys Hampton, and played it behind vocalists in Hampton's band.

segments.title: No teachers in Houston: Abner Jones and the silent-movie trio
segments.summary: Cobb calls himself self-made; the only man who could teach theory, Abner Jones, played in a silent-movie theatre trio and had no time to teach.

segments.chapter: First bands, illness and Houston life
segments.title: First summer tour with Frank Davis and the Harlem Grill with Chester Boone
segments.summary: At sixteen Cobb tours Louisiana with Frank Davis, then joins Chester Boone's band at the Harlem Grill for $34 a week while his mother earned $10; the dates are sorted out along the way.

segments.chapter: First bands, illness and Houston life
segments.title: Falling ill in Dallas with pleurisy and nearly dying
segments.summary: Cobb takes sick on a trip to Dallas, is brought home at 119 pounds, and is found to have pleurisy; a doctor treats him at home and in Jefferson Davis Hospital.

segments.chapter: First bands, illness and Houston life
segments.title: His mother's prayer and a Baptist upbringing
segments.summary: His mother tells of praying for his recovery, and Cobb says he was raised strictly Baptist.

segments.chapter: First bands, illness and Houston life
segments.title: An only child; his mother's sacrifices
segments.summary: Cobb describes being an only child, his mother boarding him out of her $10 pay, and relieving her once he earned $34.

segments.chapter: First bands, illness and Houston life
segments.title: The drugstore job and the bicycle he had to pay for
segments.summary: Cobb gets a bicycle for a $7-a-week drugstore job, eats free ice cream, and finds it deducted from his first pay.

segments.chapter: First bands, illness and Houston life
segments.title: Lesson learned: no tabs, pay as you go
segments.summary: From the ice cream incident Cobb draws his rule against running tabs, which he enforced with his own sidemen on the road.

segments.chapter: First bands, illness and Houston life
segments.title: Juneteenth in Texas and the Emancipation Day debate
segments.summary: Cobb explains that Texas blacks celebrate Emancipation on the 19th of June, and the Danceses question how it relates to other dates.

segments.chapter: First bands, illness and Houston life
segments.title: Black history month in Houston schools; Barbara Jordan
segments.summary: Cobb takes part in school clinics each February and mentions fellow Phillis Wheatley graduate Barbara Jordan.

segments.chapter: First bands, illness and Houston life
segments.title: Houston's black population and Texas history in San Antonio
segments.summary: Cobb estimates blacks at 10 to 15 percent of Houston, and talk drifts to Mexicans on the border and San Antonio's history.

segments.title: Back from the hospital: Larkin's uniform and his mother's objection
segments.summary: After the hospital Cobb rehearses with Milton Larkin, who brings his uniform; his mother protests but her sister persuades her to let him go.

segments.title: Milton Larkin watches over him and helps him buy a car
segments.summary: Larkin promised Cobb's mother to look after him, shared a house, cooked, lent $35 and showed him how to pay the car note from road trips.

segments.title: Selling insurance for Atlanta Life by day, playing with Larkin by night
segments.summary: After marrying in 1939 Cobb takes over his stepfather-in-law's insurance debit with Atlanta Life, working it while playing nights with Larkin.

segments.title: Early tenor influences: Joe Thomas above all
segments.summary: Cobb names Hawkins, Byas, Ben Webster and Joe Thomas as influences, saying Joe Thomas mattered most.

segments.title: The serenity prayer he lives by
segments.summary: Cobb recites the serenity prayer that hangs in his bedroom and Stanley Dance asks when that began.

segments.title: Told in New York he needs a second spinal operation
segments.summary: In 1947, with three months of bookings and cars bought, a doctor tells Cobb the operation must be repeated; he drives bitterly to dinner at Joe Thomas's home.

segments.title: Consulting doctors and Dr. Mayer's diagnosis of Pott's disease
segments.summary: Cobb gets a second opinion; Dr. Mayer, with agent Ben Barth present, diagnoses Pott's disease and warns of nine months in bed.

segments.title: Hit by a car at ten and hiding the injury out of fear
segments.summary: Cobb traces the bone condition to being struck by a streetcar-area car as a boy, running off so his mother wouldn't learn, and suffering for years.

segments.title: Raising his daughter and the dangers of fear and permissiveness
segments.summary: Cobb talks about his 22-year-old daughter, whom he raised after his wife's death, and about parental guidance.

segments.title: Nine months bedridden: breaking the news to the band and losing money on the cars
segments.summary: Back in the doctor's office he is told to lie flat for nine months, then tells his band in August 1947 and takes a loss on the cars.

segments.title: The members of his 1947 group who waited for him
segments.summary: Cobb lists his band: Dave Page, Booty Wood, Charlie Fowlkes, George Rhodes, Walter Buchanan and Jumping George Jones, all of whom returned when he recovered.

segments.title: Fifteen and a half months flat on his back
segments.summary: Complications, a hip problem and repeated casts and ambulance trips stretch the recovery to fifteen and a half months, two and a half years out of work.

segments.title: Ben Barth, his agent, and leaving New York in 1959
segments.summary: Cobb says agent Ben Barth treated him like a father, never asked for money back, and recalls leaving New York for Houston on June 4, 1959.

segments.title: How a newspaper prayer turned him around in the hospital
segments.summary: Bitter in the hospital, Cobb cut out the daily prayer from the Daily News and memorized it; it changed his life and remains his strength.

segments.title: Larkin's band, Cedric Haywood and Wild Bill Davis
segments.summary: Back with Milton Larkin, Cobb describes a battle of music at the Eldorado Ballroom after which Wild Bill Davis joined, and how Davis took up guitar to stay on the stand.

segments.title: Playing after-hours parties for visiting big bands; Joe Thomas as mentor
segments.summary: Larkin's band played the after parties for Lunceford, Ellington, Basie and others in Houston; Chu Berry wouldn't explain his tricks but Joe Thomas shared everything.

segments.title: The bare New York apartment and Earl Bostic's credit reference
segments.summary: Cobb and his wife take a nearly empty apartment near the Thomases; Lionel and Gladys Hampton refuse a credit reference but Earl Bostic gets him furniture credit.

segments.title: Who was in Larkin's band: Illinois Jacquet comes and goes
segments.summary: Pushed to return to Larkin, Cobb says he preceded Illinois Jacquet, who left for California in 1940 on a family railroad pass and was picked up by Hampton.

segments.title: Russell and Illinois Jacquet start out as a dance team
segments.summary: The Jacquet brothers began in Houston as dancers, and Cobb recalls root beer jobs paying 75 cents.

segments.title: Russell Jacquet's Eldorado band and the death of his wife
segments.summary: Cobb disputes that Illinois protected Russell, describing Russell's successful Houston band, his move to California and his wife's death.

segments.title: How Illinois treated his brother Russell
segments.summary: Cobb says that once Illinois formed his own band he mistreated Russell, who could have been better with proper support, and cites the Polo Grounds game snub.

segments.title: Cedric Haywood, the self-taught arranger who taught him transposition
segments.summary: Haywood taught Cobb transposition across a bed with the score, and rehearsed sections separately in different rooms until the band played from memory.

segments.title: Copying Lunceford records from the jukebox; Duke versus Lunceford
segments.summary: Larkin's band played a Lunceford record repeatedly so Haywood could chart it; Cobb admits he then preferred Lunceford to Ellington, and Cootie Williams's brother Leroy is discussed.

segments.title: Personnel of Milton Larkin's band
segments.summary: Cobb names trumpeters, trombonists, bassist, drummer and reed players who passed through Larkin's band and what became of them.

segments.title: Cootie Williams raids Larkin's band in San Antonio
segments.summary: After a fire at the Eldorado, Larkin's band moved to San Antonio where Cootie Williams hired Eddie Vinson and a trombonist but Cobb refused.

segments.title: Where the Harlem Grill was in Houston
segments.summary: Cobb locates the Harlem Grill on West Dallas near Heiner, a main Houston dance spot until the Eldorado opened in 1937.

segments.title: T-Bone Walker in Houston clubs
segments.summary: Helen Dance asks about T-Bone Walker's Houston dates; Cobb says he played the Harlem Grill and Eldorado, and mentions the Peacock run by Don Robey.

segments.title: Milton Larkin's band at the Rum Boogie in Chicago
segments.summary: In 1942 Larkin's band goes to Joe Louis's Rum Boogie in Chicago, six men short because of the draft, and stays nine months with Cobb there five.

segments.title: Taking cut of the money thrown at T-Bone Walker
segments.summary: As show director Cobb gathered the money thrown at T-Bone, who gambled it away in crap games, so he pocketed some for himself.

segments.title: Taking over as director of the Rum Boogie show band
segments.summary: With Marl Young writing and failing to get the music played, Cobb takes the baton on opening night, becomes the show's director and earns $60 a week.

segments.title: Lionel Hampton first asks him to join in 1939
segments.summary: Hampton asked Cobb to join after hearing him play Body and Soul, but Cobb asked for $500 advance and heard nothing; by 1942 Hampton wanted him again.

segments.title: Replacing Illinois Jacquet; who played tenor and alto
segments.summary: Cobb replaced Jacquet in Hampton's band and says Jacquet was an alto player whom Hampton put on tenor in 1940.

segments.title: Illinois Jacquet's gift for copying solos
segments.summary: Cobb recalls Jacquet copying Eddie Barefield's Moonglow solo after eight months on alto, and is asked whether he is original too.

segments.title: Jacquet refuses to play with him; the 1967 Austin three tenors concert
segments.summary: Cobb says Jacquet declined a battle of music, and recalls the 1967 Austin date with Jacquet and Buddy Tate, praising Tate.

segments.title: End of side four and title page of the second session
segments.summary: The tape cuts, the first session's proceedings end and a new Smithsonian title page for sides 5 to 7 begins.

segments.title: The Juneteenth haircut lie and being called Hamburger Red
segments.summary: Cobb tells how he spent his haircut money, lied to his mother, was kept from the Emancipation Park festival, and learned never to lie; his hamburger habit earned him the nickname Hamburger Red.

segments.title: Joining Lionel Hampton in San Francisco in 1942
segments.summary: Cobb goes back to take up Hampton in order, recalling the Rum Boogie manager who called him and his phone talk with Hampton, who had heard him play Body and Soul in Houston.

segments.title: Why Hampton fired Illinois Jacquet over Flying Home
segments.summary: Cobb relays what Hampton and Gladys told him: Jacquet cursed Hampton on stage for cutting off Flying Home and was given notice.

segments.title: Cliques in Hampton's band and his drinking buddies
segments.summary: Hampton's band was a syndicate of groups; Cobb fell in with Milton Buckner, Jack McVea, Fred Beckett and Al Hayes, who were drinkers rather than users.

segments.title: Al Hayes, baritone chairs and becoming straw boss
segments.summary: Cobb recalls Al Hayes and the sax section shuffle when Rudy Rutherford and Jack McVea left or fell sick, how he became straw boss and got a four-dollar raise per night.

segments.title: The Lady Be Good tenor duet with Ted McRae
segments.summary: Cobb and Ted McRae secretly rehearse a Lady Be Good duet in a Philadelphia theater break, Hampton keeps it, and Lucky Thompson, Herbie Fields and Johnny Griffin later play it.

segments.title: Playing Flying Home for Hampton and respecting the boss
segments.summary: Cobb says he started Flying Home in Houston, that Hampton let him play as long as he liked, and that he never disrespected Hampton the way Jacquet did.

segments.title: Five years with Hampton, Johnny Griffin and Hampton's love of tenor players
segments.summary: Cobb dates his Hampton years 1942 to 1947, says Johnny Griffin joined in 1945, and explains Hampton converts alto players to tenor because of Herschel Evans.

segments.title: Turning down a place in Basie's band out of fear
segments.summary: When Herschel Evans died Basie telegraphed Cobb, who declined from fear at about seventeen or eighteen, staying with his loyal family band at Larkin's.

segments.title: What Cobb learned from Joe Thomas: simplicity
segments.summary: Cobb says he is a simple player influenced by Joe Thomas's simple, effective solos, including a four-note modulation on Cheating on Me.

segments.title: Playing for the public: melody, the whistling test and keeping his own style
segments.summary: Cobb argues for playing for laymen with melodies they can whistle, criticizes too many notes in modern jazz, and insists on staying Arnett Cobb.

segments.title: Practicing on the prairie and the origin of his big tone
segments.summary: Cobb explains he practiced alone in an open field beside the house, which he feels explains his big Texas tenor tone.

segments.title: Arrangers in Hampton's band: Milton Buckner, Al Hayes, Joe Morris
segments.summary: Buckner wrote most of the band's arrangements, Al Hayes wrote Loose Wigs, and Joe Morris wrote Chop-Chop.

segments.title: Curly Hamner's royalty check and Cobb's unpaid tune
segments.summary: Cobb complains that Curly Hamner, Gladys and Hampton each got $2,200 on a tune Milton Buckner wrote and that he never received royalties on his own copyrighted tune.

segments.title: Cobb's Hampton contract and the first-class train ride that never came
segments.summary: Cobb describes signing a second two-year contract in a California lawyer's office promising first-class travel, billing and financing, which Hampton mostly did not honor.

segments.title: Gladys Hampton, Benny Goodman and Hampton's Christian Science
segments.summary: Cobb tells how Gladys looked after Hampton, was hired for Goodman's care at $150 a week, and kept Hampton away from hangers-on until he turned to Christian Science.

segments.title: Hampton's endless rehearsals and the cattle-car trip to Oakland
segments.summary: Hampton called rehearsals out of loneliness; after a night on a cattle car the band reached Oakland at four and was told to rehearse at six.

segments.title: Joe Wilder tells off Hampton; his classical background
segments.summary: Joe Wilder, mild-mannered and always warmed up early, fell out with Hampton over a rehearsal; Cobb notes Wilder was a trained cornetist who once sat in with Dizzy.

segments.title: Newcomers Cobb and Joe Wilder isolated in Hampton's band
segments.summary: Wilder and Cobb joined together in San Francisco, roomed together, were left out by the band's cliques, and Wilder won respect by sight-reading a hard chart.

segments.title: Selfish musicians in New York today
segments.summary: Cobb complains that New York musicians keep to themselves, contrasting it with his own hospitality in Houston.

segments.title: The buzzard roof at the Majestic and disillusion with idols in New York
segments.summary: Cobb recalls sitting in the segregated roof of Houston's Majestic Theater to see the big bands, then finding the same stars short of money in New York, which made him begin to save.

segments.title: Lucky Thompson's quarrel with Gladys at the Famous Door in 1943
segments.summary: Lucky Thompson, cocky after three years on the horn, asks Gladys to pay for a new horn, and after the Famous Door engagement ends over unpaid wages he and his wife curse her.

segments.title: Gladys buys Cobb the horn Lucky Thompson wanted
segments.summary: Gladys sends Cobb to Manning's to pick a used horn for $265, which turns out to be the one Lucky had chosen; Cobb also talks about his Selmer and Yamaha horns.

segments.title: Lucky Thompson gets his notice; his attitude and exile
segments.summary: Lucky showed up with a clarinet and was fired; Cobb says his attitude blocked bookings and drove him to Europe, whereas it is best to be congenial.

segments.title: Charlie Parker and the pro-rated contract
segments.summary: Cobb recalls that Parker, paid $1,750 a week at Birdland, often failed to show until his contract was pro-rated.

segments.title: Fred Beckett's illness and death
segments.summary: Cobb tells how Fred Beckett, a heavy drinker with tuberculosis, overstayed a hospital pass and died in St. Louis.

segments.title: Fred Beckett's plunger-mute melody playing
segments.summary: Hampton featured Beckett playing straight melody with a plunger mute into the microphone before a Ruby Blakely vocal, a style Cobb likens to Johnny Hodges.

segments.title: Duke Garrett arrives from the Navy to meet Hampton
segments.summary: Duke Garrett, a trumpeter and ex-Navy man whose brother-in-law ran a Black press service, came to New York to join Hampton and Cobb unwittingly introduced him.

segments.title: Dave Page fired and Cobb wrongly blamed
segments.summary: After Garrett got his audition Dave Page was given notice, bandmates blamed Cobb, and the gangster-like atmosphere helped him decide to leave; Page was his first trumpeter later.

segments.title: Money lending and crap games in Hampton's band
segments.summary: Cobb says Duke handled loans at interest while Gladys stopped draws, so Cobb ran crap games and lent money too, lending Lamar Wright $20 in a game.

segments.title: The great Hampton band and Herbie Fields's Fort Dix background
segments.summary: Cobb lists key members of Hampton's best band, including Milton Buckner, Charlie Harris and Sinclair, then explains who Herbie Fields was before joining.

segments.title: MCA exploits Herbie Fields until Joe Glazer places him with Hampton
segments.summary: Cobb relates how MCA bled Fields's family out of $80,000 for air time and passed him over for another act until Joe Glazer rescued him and put him with Hampton at $250 a week.

segments.title: Refused service at Leo Poole's bar in San Francisco
segments.summary: Cobb, his wife and Herbie Fields were refused service at a bar in the war years, and a suit they filed brought $100 that they gave to the NAACP.

segments.title: Herbie Fields as a friend; his suicide and Hampton's pay scale
segments.summary: Cobb remembers Fields as a warm roommate, is shocked when he reads of Fields's suicide in Miami, and recalls seeing Fields's $250 pay stub when he himself made $175.

segments.title: Not materialistic: why he doesn't hoard money
segments.summary: Cobb says he wants only enough to live on, noting that Howard Hughes could not take his money with him.

segments.title: Does a player's horn tell his message? Herbie Fields's playing
segments.summary: Dance wonders whether Fields was frustrated by his playing lacking feeling and Cobb agrees that a player expresses what is on his mind through his horn.

segments.title: Earl Bostic asks why he can't get a break
segments.summary: Bostic visits Cobb after his spinal operation and asks why he never gets breaks; Cobb tells him people can't relate to so many notes and to play more melodically.

segments.title: Earl Bostic runs Kermit Scott off the stand
segments.summary: At a Harlem club Bostic sat in and called Eliza in E flat, rising a half step each chorus, which drove Kermit Scott off his own job.

segments.title: Snooky Young in Hampton's band
segments.summary: Dance asks about Snooky Young and Cobb praises him as a good trumpeter with a round tone.

segments.title: Deciding to leave Hampton in 1947 and planning to rest
segments.summary: After a Pittsburgh Courier night at Carnegie Hall, Cobb resolves to leave, using his back as an excuse, after the Wantz brothers book him for Easter and Gladys objects that it didn't come through her.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Title page for sides 9 to 12 of the third session
segments.summary: The Smithsonian title page and transcription service notices for the next session, with the Danceses picking up in Cleveland.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Handing in his notice in Cleveland with a detective as witness
segments.summary: In Cleveland Cobb gives Hampton written notice with a detective friend present as witness and plays one show before Johnny Griffin takes over.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: The gangster atmosphere in Hampton's band that drove him out
segments.summary: Cobb describes Curly Hamner, the masseur and the valet carrying a pistol for Hampton, cursing in front of wives, and says it broke up a good band.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Why he left: monopoly over his outside work and fear for his wife
segments.summary: Cobb explains he left because Hampton and Gladys wanted every booking to come through them, and he took a witness because he feared the notice would be denied.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: The Zanzibar in Philadelphia and Gale Agency's Ralph Cooper
segments.summary: His two-week Philadelphia job packs the club, agents Ralph Cooper and Lou Leslie hear him, and Cooper pushes him over breakfast to sign with Gale Agency instead of resting.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Signing a one-year contract with Gale Agency; Billy Shaw and Charlie Parker
segments.summary: Cobb signs a year instead of the three Billy Shaw wanted, as Charlie Parker walks in.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: The Baby Grand Cafe on April 29 and his first record contract
segments.summary: Cobb's group fills in for Billie Holiday at Harlem's Baby Grand, nearly gets fired for being loud, is kept, and gets a recording contract with Apollo.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Billy Shaw's Gale days and the first small band
segments.summary: Cobb sorts out when Billy Shaw worked for Gale, says he worked seven months until January 1948, and lists his five-piece rhythm section with Dave Page and later Booty Wood.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: First Apollo records of 1947: When I Grow Too Old to Dream and Go, Red, Go
segments.summary: Cobb names the sides cut before the recording ban, including Part One and Two of When I Grow Too Old to Dream with Booty Wood, and a later Jersey date paid on the spot.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Dutch Kitchen Bounce, Bob Causer's credit and refusing outside publishers
segments.summary: Cobb explains how Cornell's Bob Causer got title credit for two tunes, and why he refused to let another publisher control Dutch Kitchen Bounce after being cheated over Tempo and Swing.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Eddie Barefield punches him in the back at the Apollo
segments.summary: At Christmas 1946, backstage at the Apollo, a drunken Barefield punches Cobb in the back; Cobb says he only told him last week and blames it for his later operation.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Pott's disease and the March 1948 operation
segments.summary: Cobb explains the bone fusion operation he entered on March 1, 1948, how a fall and a car injury together caused the disease, and that he stayed out two and a half years.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Insurance coverage that paid his hospital bills
segments.summary: Cobb says good insurance covered his hospitalization and, from his Atlanta Life days, he stays insurance conscious for his family.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Lying in bed: no pain, just helplessness
segments.summary: Asked about the frustration of bed rest, Cobb says there was little pain after the first days, just the dependence on nurses turning and rubbing him.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Convalescing at home with Dr. Mayer's exercises
segments.summary: Dr. Mayer visited Cobb's Long Island house and gave him seven weeks of exercises so he could walk on a walker and crutches.

segments.chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
segments.title: Dr. Leo Mayer, the humanitarian who refused payment
segments.summary: Cobb praises Dr. Mayer, Roosevelt's doctor, who would not take the $500 offered of the $1,500 owed, and remembers him courting after his wife died.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Rebuilding the band and a package show with Dinah Washington
segments.summary: After recovery Cobb re-forms his band without Booty Wood and Charlie Fowlkes and goes out with Lamar Wright Jr. on a Dinah Washington package show booked by Universal.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Ben Barth's death and how Cobb brought James Brown to Universal
segments.summary: Cobb says Ben Barth died in 1966, and that Barth signed James Brown after Cobb screened him in Macon, Georgia.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: James Brown package tour and the Fillmore flop on Easter 1958
segments.summary: Cobb leads the band on a California tour with James Brown and Little Willie John, plays to 200 people at the Fillmore, and has to wire Universal money to bail the band out of a hotel.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Disbanding in 1959 after eight years on the road
segments.summary: Cobb disbanded in February 1959 after a last job in Philadelphia and confirms he had led his own band for Universal from about 1950 until his 1956 accident.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: The weekend in Providence before the crash
segments.summary: Cobb and his wife drive their new DeSoto with baby Lisette to Providence's Celebrity Club, scouting entertainers, and stay an extra day.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Blacking out at the wheel near Hartford, April 23, 1956
segments.summary: On the drive south of Hartford, Cobb chokes on saliva, blacks out and hits a tree at a filling station, breaking his leg and cutting his mouth while the baby is bumped.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: His wife's lung damage and the day before her death in 1970
segments.summary: Cobb links his wife's collapsed lungs to the crash, and recalls arranging to pick up Joe Thomas on February 12, 1970.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: The night his wife Elizabeth died of a hemorrhage
segments.summary: Cobb relates the evening of February 1970: toast, a cough, bleeding, her death, and telling his daughter.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: What caused the blackout, and the rescue at the crash site
segments.summary: A doctor told Cobb that choking cut oxygen to his brain; he describes the tourist doctor's help, his pinned legs and seeing his baby.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Three months in Hartford Hospital and his wife's fight to get home to the baby
segments.summary: Cobb woke in traction; his wife, who had lost earlier pregnancies, fought to recover and went home with a broken arm to care for baby Lisette.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Hospital stitches and lost teeth, with the anniversary on the ward
segments.summary: Their anniversary passes in the hospital, a doctor's lip repair draws admiring staff, and Cobb lost six teeth and more since.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Hartford doctors send him home and Dr. Mayer takes over again
segments.summary: Refusing amputation, Cobb is sent home by ambulance, stays in bed through the summer, then enters Hospital for Joint Disease under Dr. Mayer from October 1956 to January 1957.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Therapy in the pool, a shorter leg and a built-up shoe
segments.summary: After the cast, Cobb relearns movement, discovers the Hartford surgeons left his leg short, and gets a lift in his shoe made first in leather and then cork.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Back and hip unharmed; Lisette's first birthday
segments.summary: Cobb says the fused areas held and only the leg was damaged; he left the hospital the day after his daughter's first birthday and did not work until June 1957.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: A new seven-piece band and learning to play on crutches
segments.summary: Cobb forms a seven-piece band with Dickie Harris, Harold Cumberbatch and Eddie Lewis (nicknamed Tiger), and explains how he still needs crutches on steps.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Going back to work despite doctors' warnings
segments.summary: Cobb says the doctors once said he'd die, but trusting God he returned to work with Dr. Mayer's permission; his first job was Philadelphia's 21 Club in a walking cast, earning the nickname Speedy.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Ben Barth stood by him; why he carries heavy insurance
segments.summary: Cobb says Ben Barth stayed in his corner and he never borrowed from him, helped by insurance that he still carries heavily.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Coast to coast on crutches, then giving up and returning to Houston in 1959
segments.summary: Cobb worked from 1957 to February 1959, twice crossing the country on crutches, then quit and flew home to Houston with his daughter on June 4.

segments.chapter: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
segments.title: Bailing out the band in Texas after the Joe Louis fight week
segments.summary: On the Linda Hopkins, James Brown and Little Willie John show, Cobb handled the master contract and had to send for money, and a hotel manager gave him a free week for playing a post-fight party.

segments.chapter: Back in Houston, Club Ebony and Boo Pleasant
segments.title: Taking over the Club Ebony in January 1960
segments.summary: Back in Houston, Cobb and his wife take over management of Club Ebony around the corner from his house and use his band as house band.

segments.chapter: Back in Houston, Club Ebony and Boo Pleasant
segments.title: The twenty-five-cent Blue Monday sessions
segments.summary: Cobb describes starting Blue Monday afternoons at 25 cents a head, filling the club with off-day workers and visiting jammers and raising the register.

segments.chapter: Back in Houston, Club Ebony and Boo Pleasant
segments.title: Hiring pianist Boo Pleasant from San Antonio
segments.summary: Cobb tells how he heard Boo Pleasant play in San Antonio, auditioned her in Houston, and brought her to Chicago where she stayed two years and drew men to the club.

segments.chapter: Back in Houston, Club Ebony and Boo Pleasant
segments.title: What became of Boo Pleasant and her children
segments.summary: Boo left the band, fell into a bad crowd, and Cobb and his wife had tried to help raise her children; her son was shot in a park and later died.

segments.chapter: Back in Houston, Club Ebony and Boo Pleasant
segments.title: Boo's mother kills her father in Corpus Christi in 1954
segments.summary: On the way to open at the Eldorado in August 1954 Boo learns her alcoholic mother shot her father, Corpus Christi's Black politician, and no trial followed.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: Refusing and then accepting the invitation to tour Europe
segments.summary: Cobb explains he turned down European tours while his wife lived, until his mother urged him to answer, and in 1973 the organizers arranged help for him.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: First European tour in 1973 with Black and Blue
segments.summary: Cobb describes the 1973 package show for the Black and Blue organizers, with Milton Buckner, Candy Johnson, Helen Humes, Al Casey and others.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: The 1974 tour and the first Montreux Festival
segments.summary: Cobb says he first played Montreux last year, went again in 1974 with Tiny Grimes and Panama Francis, and mentions seeing Sir Charles Thompson in Boston.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: The nine-piece band of 1976 with two tenors
segments.summary: Cobb lists the 1976 European nine-piece band and recalls the opening head arrangement, Jumpin' with Symphony Sid, and tenor battles with Eddie Chamblee.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: Candy Johnson's search for Ben Webster
segments.summary: On the tour Candy Johnson tracked down Ben Webster in Denmark with Johnny Simmons's help, spent four days with him, and Webster died two weeks later.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: How the European tours travel: buses and fast drivers
segments.summary: Cobb denies the story of standing for 200 miles, says the organizers' reclining-seat bus beats cars driven fast by Jean-Pierre, and that the tour never travels at night.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: Roseland Ballroom, the Nice triumph and the coming Hampton trip
segments.summary: Cobb recalls the 1977 Roseland concert with Sy Oliver, the next-day flight to Nice where he was called star of the show, and the schedule for returning to Nice with Hampton.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: The Boston tribute to Hampton and the young drummer Terri Lyne Carrington
segments.summary: Cobb lists the all-star band at the March 15 Boston tribute to Lionel Hampton and praises a twelve-year-old girl drummer while fearing she is pushed too fast.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: A snowbound trip back from Boston and carrying his horn
segments.summary: Cobb describes being helped by friend Doc Nepples, the Houston flight being diverted to Kennedy Airport in the snow, and how he packs his horn.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: Arnett Cobb and the Mobb at the Zanzibar; Charlie Barnet breaks his horn
segments.summary: At the Zanzibar a Daily News critic called Cobb's six-piece group a mob, giving the name the Mobb, while Charlie Barnet bent his soprano sax over his leg in a domestic row.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: Birdland engagements and the discovery of copied arrangements
segments.summary: Cobb describes his graduated Birdland contract, then finds that George Rhodes and Reuben Phillips sold his scores to Willis Jackson, who played the same charts.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: A miserable two weeks opposite Willis Jackson
segments.summary: Cobb and Jackson follow each other on stage with the same arrangements, he fumes and tap dances to compensate, and he demands the scores from his arrangers afterward.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: Dinah Washington's Christmas gifts to him in the hospital
segments.summary: Dinah Washington sends Cobb liquor, a television and $50 while he is in Hospital for Joint Disease at Christmas 1956.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: Dinah Washington's respect for her mother, Ms. Jones
segments.summary: Cobb says Dinah, born Ruth Jones, bought her mother a home and a car for her stepfather but would only be meek around her mother.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: Dinah Washington pulls a pistol on Hampton
segments.summary: Furious that Hampton wouldn't let her record vocals, Dinah drinks gin, fetches a pistol without a firing pin and threatens Hampton, after which Gladys ends her ten-year $75 contract.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: Ben Barth made Dinah a star; the Keynote session at the Apollo
segments.summary: Cobb says Ben Barth built Dinah's career, and recalls a Keynote session at the Apollo with Buckner that ran until 5 a.m., and his own hustle selling Swing Books.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: His mother's final illness and death in December 1975
segments.summary: Cobb speaks of his mother as wise confidant who came to live with him after his wife died, her stroke in November 1975 and death on December 17, and her protectiveness of him.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: Norma leaves him and returns
segments.summary: Cobb says his present wife Norma left on October 6, 1975 after his drinking and arguments, stayed away two years and then phoned to say she missed him.

segments.chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
segments.title: Directions to the club and his current group at Club La Bicque
segments.summary: The Danceses get directions to Club La Bicque on Blodgett, where Cobb has played three years with Kenny Andrews, Ben Turner and Larry Slezak, and the recording ends.
